items.title: Switzerland Confirms First AI-Agent Cyberattacks on Local Organisations
items.summary: Switzerland reports its first AI-agent cyberattacks, including critical infrastructure breaches, and urges patching internet-facing systems within 24 hours. Switzerland ’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has now seen these attacks firsthand. In recent days, it received its first reports of cyberattacks on Swiss organisations carried out with the help of AI agents. The victims include critical infrastructure operators in at least two sectors. “In recent days, the NCSC has received its first reports of cyberattacks against organisations in Switzerland in which the attack was carried out with the assistance of an AI agent.” reads the report published by NCSC. “Various organisations and operators of critical infrastructure across at least two sectors have been affected by these cyberattacks.” What stands out is the result. In every AI-assisted attack known to the NCSC, the attackers successfully compromised the victims’ IT systems. The agency sees these incidents as more than isolated cases, warning that they mark a shift in the cyber threat landscape. The attackers used what the NCSC calls “Agentic Offensive Frameworks”. These AI agents can search for vulnerabilities, choose attack tools, assess the results and decide what to do next, all with limited human input. Security teams also use the same software for penetration testing, which makes these tools dual-use. The targets aren’t exotic. The agents go after standard or easily guessed passwords, known flaws in software, and systems connected to the internet. “AI agents often require only a fraction of the time a human would need to locate such vulnerable systems and exploit existing vulnerabilities. Furthermore, they can react flexibly to defence mechanisms by switching to other known attack methods. This leaves organisations with significantly less time to detect an attack and respond appropriately.” continues the report. AI agents can quickly switch tactics when a defence blocks an attack, leaving organisations less time to detect and stop intrusions. The NCSC warns that these tools speed up common attack methods and that internet-accessible agents such as ARTEX and CyberStrikeAI have almost doubled since October 2026. This could lead to more frequent, faster and more successful automated attacks against organisations of all types. ARTEX isn’t a surprise. The FBI recently published a FLASH alert that describes it as open source, with no model of its own, plugged into external language models. The same advisory says some intrusions went from first contact to privileged access in under three hours. The NCSC expects more successful attacks and urges companies and critical infrastructure operators to strengthen their security and resilience. It monitors the threat landscape, stays in contact with national and international partners, and shares technical indicators for detecting these tools with infrastructure operators. Its recommendations are short, and it wants them applied without delay. Start by shrinking what’s exposed. Fewer systems facing the internet means a smaller attack surface, and where possible you can restrict access with geo-blocking or an allow list of IP addresses or network segments. Every internal resource reachable from the internet, such as webmail and VPN, should sit behind multi-factor authentication or passkeys, with no exceptions. Then limit the damage. Grant the lowest access rights that work, and watch for deviations from normal behaviour and data volumes across identities, applications, workloads and infrastructure. Test your own infrastructure for vulnerabilities on a regular basis, yourself or with an outside specialist. “Critical security updates for systems accessible via the internet should be installed as soon as possible, but no later than 24 hours after release.” concludes the report. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Switzerland)

items.title: Broadcom issues fixes for 23 new VMware flaws, three critical
items.summary: Broadcom on Tuesday reported almost two dozen new security vulnerabilities in VMware, adding to a lengthy list of fixes from this month alone. The most serious of the flaws in the current advisory is a vCenter authentication bypass vulnerability, CVE-2026-123903, assigned a CVSSv3 base score of 9.8 (Critical). “A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system,” it said. In a supplemental document accompanying the alert , Broadcom noted that because of coordinated disclosure and release pipeline timing, the advisory comes just two days before the US Thanksgiving holiday, admitting, “this timing is not optimal.” The company said that the advisory covers a total of 23 issues, seven of which are in vCenter: an authentication bypass and three denial-of-service issues in the VMware Directory Service, an arbitrary file write while processing certain archives, a local privilege escalation in a vpxd service script, and a security policy enforcement failure in the vSphere Distributed Switch (vDS). Seven more are in ESX: a heap out-of-bounds write and a use-after-free in the I/O filter service, an out-of-bounds write in the Extensible Host Controller Interface (XHCI) USB controller, a stack-based buffer overflow in the VMkernel, a security bypass in the host configuration store, a signature verification bypass, and a denial of service in guest RPC. The remaining flaws affect VMware Workstation, VMware Fusion, VMware Tools, and VMware Avi Load Balancer. However, the company noted that the fixes delivered to address the flaws in last week’s advisory resolve some of the issues highlighted in the current batch. “If you applied vCenter 8.0 U3m for VMSA-2026-0009 , including on VCF 5.2.x, you do not need to update vCenter again, but vCenter 9.1.x needs the update in this advisory,” Broadcom said. “ESX was not part of VMSA-2026-0009 and needs the update in this advisory. VMSA-2026-0009 also resolved issues in SDDC Manager, which this advisory does not update. If you have not applied the SDDC Manager update from VMSA-2026-0009, apply it separately. This advisory also includes a VMware Tools update. Updating vCenter and ESX does not update VMware Tools inside virtual machines, so plan that update separately.” It added, “if you have a question about whether you are affected, it is likely that you are and should take action immediately.” Difference of opinion on patching urgency So is this a signal to interrupt the US Thanksgiving holiday to address the flaws? Opinions differ. Tyler Reguly , Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, argued that although a 9.8 score is about as high as they get, the nature of the holes might not merit extreme scheduling. There are three vulnerabilities rated 9.8 in severity listed in the current batch, affecting VMware vCenter and ESX. He pointed out, “neither of these [affected] systems should be present on your external interfaces, so the risk would need to be internal. That means we’re talking about an inside threat or a breach that is already underway. These are important vulnerabilities, so there’s no doubt about that, but they are not so important that anyone should interrupt their holiday weekend.” Reguly suggested a strict interpretation of CISA guidance to support his contention that these patches may not merit emergency response. “If we take a look at CISA BOD-26-04 as our guidance on this, is the service publicly exposed? It shouldn’t be, so let’s say no. Is this vulnerability in the KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog]? No. Could it be automated? Unknown, so let’s assume yes for safety’s sake,” he said. “A result of No, No, and Yes translates to line 13 on the BOD-26-04 remediation timelines, which allows for 60 days to fix the issue.” He observed that the recent onslaught of vulnerabilities has made us “a bit like Pavlov’s dog:” We’ve been conditioned to react every time we see CVSS 9.8. “This is a dangerous and potentially harmful conditioning that we need to make every effort to break,” he said. “We need to remind ourselves that the severity of a vulnerability does not reflect risk to an organization, just as the bell did not represent food.” Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, disagreed. He considered the current advisory, VMSA-2026-0011, to be “a big deal because it hits vCenter and ESX, the two systems that run every virtual machine, with flaws that need no password. Skip the patch, and one attacker can take down or take over every virtual machine you run. You are essentially toast. Patch now.” Dickson noted that this batch of alerts contains multiple problematic security issues, which include authentication bypass in vCenter; permitting an attacker with network access to run code on the hypervisor itself; and another bug that lets an administrator inside a virtual machine on Workstation or Fusion run code on the host computer. “Let’s face it: AI loves to chain vulnerabilities,” he said. He is also worried about the large number of VMware patches this month alone, especially those in vCenter. “The frequency of VMware’s vCenter flaws is a concern, as they keep landing in the same place,” he said. “The new flaw is distinct from last week’s. Distinct is not comforting. Three different holes in the same wall is a wall problem.” He pointed out, “The directory service has become vCenter’s Achilles’ heel. This advisory adds three denial-of-service flaws in the same service for good measure.”

items.title: How to Evaluate a Threat Intelligence Platform in 2027
items.summary: Table Of Contents Table of Contents What Is a Threat Intelligence Platform? Seven Key Criteria for Evaluating a Threat Intelligence Platform in 2027 Five Questions to Ask During a Threat Intelligence Platform Demo Common Mistakes to Avoid When Comparing Threat Intelligence Platforms Frequently Asked Questions Choosing the Right Threat Intelligence Platform for 2027 More subscribe to our newsletter Threat intelligence teams are being asked to monitor more threats, support more use cases, and deliver faster answers, often without additional resources. According to Flashpoint’s Enterprise Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 , 65% of respondents identified alert noise and false positives as a top-three challenge affecting their programs. Another 55% cited insufficient analyst bandwidth, while 50% pointed to tool integration and interoperability challenges. Meanwhile, the threat landscape continues to expand. Flashpoint’s Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition found that infostealers harvested more than 1.7 billion credentials from 7.4 million infected devices in the first half of 2026. More than 21,000 vulnerabilities were disclosed during the same period, 19% of which already had public or functional exploit code. Threat actors also posted more than 22 million times about AI toolkits intended for criminal use. For organizations evaluating threat intelligence platforms in 2027, the challenge is finding a solution that can turn this growing volume of information into relevant intelligence that security teams can investigate and act on. This guide covers seven criteria to consider when comparing threat intelligence platforms, questions to ask prospective vendors, and how to evaluate their capabilities against your organization’s security priorities. What Is a Threat Intelligence Platform? A threat intelligence platform (TIP) is technology that helps organizations collect, analyze, and act on information about current and emerging threats. Security teams use these platforms to support threat detection, incident response, vulnerability management, fraud prevention, and executive protection. Threat intelligence solutions generally fall into two broad models. Traditional TIPs aggregate indicators of compromise (IOCs) from multiple third-party feeds and distribute them to security tools. More comprehensive threat intelligence platforms collect intelligence directly from the sources where threats originate, combining that data with finished analysis, investigation tools, alerting, and integrations. The distinction matters because indicators alone rarely explain whether a threat affects a particular organization. A feed containing millions of IOCs may offer less immediate value than a verified alert identifying an employee’s compromised credentials, the source of the exposure, and the information needed to investigate. Flashpoint Ignite is an example of a comprehensive threat intelligence platform, combining Flashpoint Primary Source Collection, finished intelligence, investigation capabilities, and integrations across cyber threat intelligence, vulnerability intelligence, fraud, physical security, and brand protection. “Flashpoint has the most comprehensive deep and dark web coverage we’ve seen to date.” Senior Advisor, Incident Response Seven Key Criteria for Evaluating a Threat Intelligence Platform in 2027 1. Intelligence Coverage and Source Access Start by examining where a provider collects intelligence and how much visibility it maintains into the environments where threats originate. Threat actors operate across illicit forums, marketplaces, encrypted messaging channels, ransomware leak sites, and infostealer log shops. Intelligence collected from these sources can expose compromised credentials, planned attacks, emerging exploits, and other threats before they appear in an organization’s internal security telemetry. However, vendors that advertise coverage of the same source categories may differ considerably in the depth, continuity, and historical reach of their collection. Questions to ask when evaluating intelligence coverage: Source diversity: Does the provider collect intelligence from the open, deep, and dark web, including restricted forums, illicit marketplaces, and messaging platforms? Historical visibility: How far back can analysts search to investigate recurring activity, relationships between threat actors, and changes in behavior? Collection continuity: How does the provider maintain visibility when communities migrate, restrict access, or shut down? Organizational relevance: Does the intelligence cover the threat actors, industries, geographic regions, and assets that matter to your organization? How Flashpoint addresses it Flashpoint Primary Source Collection gathers intelligence directly from the digital environments where threats originate, including open and hard-to-reach sources. Its collection supports investigations across illicit communities, marketplaces, messaging platforms, and other environments where adversaries exchange information. In The Forrester Wave : External Threat Intelligence Service Providers, Q3 2026 , where Flashpoint was named a customer favorite, Forrester described Flashpoint as ideal for customers seeking primary-source access intelligence, particularly in the financial industry. Flashpoint Ignite also supports priority intelligence requirements (PIRs), helping teams align their intelligence collection and monitoring with the risks most relevant to their organizations. 2. Intelligence Quality and Analytical Expertise Access to threat data is only valuable when analysts can determine which findings are credible, relevant, and worth investigating. In Flashpoint’s Enterprise Threat Intelligence Report, 65% of respondents cited alert noise and false positives among their top three operational challenges. Intelligence quality therefore has a direct impact on analyst capacity. Outdated, duplicated, or poorly contextualized findings can create additional investigations without improving an organization’s understanding of risk. Look at how each provider validates collected information, enriches indicators, connects related datasets, and communicates confidence in its assessments. Questions to ask when evaluating intelligence quality: Validation: How does the provider verify findings and assess source credibility? Analytical context: Does the platform provide finished intelligence alongside raw data and technical indicators? Evidence transparency: Can analysts access the underlying sources supporting an alert or assessment? Expert support: Can customers submit requests for information (RFIs) or consult the provider’s intelligence analysts? Confidence assessments: How does the provider distinguish confirmed activity from preliminary reporting or lower-confidence findings? How Flashpoint addresses it Flashpoint combines primary-source intelligence with analysis from a multilingual team of intelligence professionals. Within Ignite, analysts can investigate underlying evidence, review finished intelligence, and submit RFIs when they need additional context or deeper research. This combination of collection and analyst expertise is particularly valuable when investigations require understanding adversary behavior, underground communities, or emerging threats that have not yet been widely documented. As one Flashpoint customer, a senior cybersecurity engineer in the healthcare and biotech industry, explained: “Flashpoint is a world class threat intelligence vendor. They offer insights into the DDW that no other intelligence providers can. Additionally, Flashpoint provides access to their analysts with RFIs which provide a much deeper and thorough understanding of any topic that we need further information on.” Sr. Cybersecurity Engineer Healthcare and Biotech 3. Actionability and Integration With Security Workflows Threat intelligence needs to reach the systems and people responsible for taking action. Even highly relevant findings can lose value when analysts must manually transfer information between disconnected tools. In Flashpoint’s Enterprise Threat Intelligence Report, 50% of respondents identified tool integration and interoperability as a top-three challenge affecting their threat intelligence programs. The report also describes how manual handoffs between intelligence feeds, SIEMs, SOAR platforms, ticketing systems, and response workflows consume analyst time. These gaps can delay investigations and make it harder to consistently apply intelligence across security operations. When evaluating a platform, examine how intelligence moves from discovery through validation, prioritization, and response. Questions to ask when evaluating integrations: Existing technology: Does the platform integrate with your SIEM, SOAR, EDR, vulnerability management, and ticketing systems? Integration methods: Does it support APIs, prebuilt connectors, machine-readable feeds, and standards such as STIX and TAXII? Workflow enrichment: Can intelligence add context to existing alerts, investigations, and incident response processes? Asset-specific alerting: Can teams configure alerts around their organization’s domains, brands, executives, and technologies? Operational efficiency: Can the platform reduce duplicate findings, unnecessary manual steps, and irrelevant alerts? During a demonstration, ask the vendor to show a realistic workflow. For example, what happens when an employee’s credentials appear in a newly collected infostealer log? Can the platform identify the exposure, provide supporting context, and deliver the information to the team responsible for remediation? How Flashpoint addresses it Flashpoint Ignite supports intelligence sharing through APIs, STIX/TAXII, MISP, and integrations with established security and investigation platforms. These include SIEM and SOAR tools such as Splunk, QRadar, Elastic, and Cortex XSOAR; threat intelligence platforms such as Anomali ThreatStream and ThreatConnect; and ServiceNow security workflows. Ignite also supports alerts based on organizational assets and intelligence requirements, helping teams route relevant findings into existing operational processes. A Flashpoint customer in the financial sector described how these capabilities support its security program: “Flashpoint has been an integral part of our threat intelligence and hunting program. We leverage their data feeds to our SIEM for correlation against all ingress/egress traffic and use their reports and daily stand-ups to update our executive committee on the latest trends in the cyber industry.” Global Head of Information Security Financial Sector 4. Threat Intelligence Capabilities by Use Case The right threat intelligence platform depends on the risks an organization needs to monitor. A financial institution managing account takeover and payment fraud may prioritize compromised credentials and illicit marketplaces. A critical infrastructure operator may need deeper visibility into vulnerability exploitation, ransomware groups, and physical security threats. Begin with your organization’s priority use cases, then assess how well each vendor supports them. Questions to ask when evaluating use-case coverage: Priority alignment: Which of our highest-priority intelligence requirements can the platform address? Depth of coverage: How much relevant intelligence and investigative context is available for each use case? Cross-functional visibility: Can different teams use the same intelligence foundation to investigate related threats? Specialized capabilities: Does the platform provide the monitoring, analysis, and response support needed for our particular risks? Expansion: Can we add new use cases as our security requirements evolve? How Flashpoint addresses it Flashpoint Ignite supports intelligence workflows spanning cyber threat intelligence, vulnerability intelligence, compromised credentials, ransomware, fraud, physical security, and brand protection. For vulnerability management teams, Flashpoint provides exploitability intelligence, evidence of active exploitation, and risk-based signals to help prioritize remediation. Its known exploited vulnerability catalog also tracks exploitation activity beyond vulnerabilities included in CISA’s KEV catalog. For fraud teams, Flashpoint provides visibility into illicit marketplaces, compromised accounts, and emerging schemes. Physical security and executive protection teams can use intelligence from online environments to investigate potential threats to people, facilities, and events. Flashpoint received the highest possible scores in the Fraud Intelligence and Executive Protection criteria in The Forrester Wave : External Threat Intelligence Service Providers, Q3 2026 . 5. AI and Agentic Capabilities AI is becoming an increasingly important consideration in threat intelligence platform evaluations. Flashpoint’s Enterprise Threat Intelligence Report found that 45% of respondents were already using or piloting agentic AI in their threat intelligence workflows, while another 35% planned to adopt it within the next 12 to 24 months. Organizations are exploring AI to reduce repetitive work, accelerate investigations, and help analysts manage expanding intelligence requirements. At the same time, the research found that teams are setting high expectations for accuracy, transparency, and control. Some threat intelligence platforms use machine learning for classification and pattern detection. Others incorporate generative AI for natural-language search, summarization, and reporting. Agentic capabilities extend further, supporting multi-step workflows such as investigations, alert triage, and intelligence briefings. The distinction matters when evaluating how much work a platform can perform and what oversight those activities require. A threat intelligence platform (TIP) is technology that helps organizations collect, analyze, and act on information about current and emerging threats. items.title: Discord’s December Privacy Update: Ad IDs for Quests, Public Messages for Its Models
items.summary: Discord’s new privacy terms take effect on 15 December. They bring advertising IDs to its Quests ads and say public messages in big servers can help build its models. Discord posted the update on 23 November. Its summary page lists age checks, public server pages on the web, partner perks and a fuller explanation of its machine learning, and says most of it isn’t new. Advertising IDs aren’t mentioned. We compared the new Privacy Policy with the September 2025 version in Discord’s own archive, and the help pages Discord edited on 23 November with copies the Wayback Machine saved earlier this month. On 25 November the changes were being picked apart on Bluesky and the Privacy Guides forum; we found no coverage by a news outlet. We’ve asked Discord for comment.

items.title: China Unicom Fiber Modem Runs a Hidden Data-Collection Plugin and a Police-Audit Stack, Researcher Says
items.summary: A ZTE fiber modem supplied by China Unicom carries two separate surveillance systems, according to a teardown published on 25 November. One is the carrier’s own data-collection plugin. It logs every device in the home, the sites each one visits, and account numbers and search terms pulled from unencrypted web traffic, using a built-in list of 743 rules for 208 Chinese websites. The other comes from Surfilter, a Shenzhen company whose products include network security audit systems, and the researcher says it is built for police audit logging. The write-up appeared in three parts on net4people/bbs , a GitHub forum used by censorship researchers, at 16:43 UTC. It follows an 18 November post about a similar plugin in China Telecom modems, which the Chinese forum V2EX has since hidden. When we published, the Unicom findings had no coverage outside that thread, and we found no major outlet that had covered the Telecom one either. We checked the files the researcher published (chapter 3) and have asked China Unicom, ZTE and Surfilter for comment.

items.summary: Series ConclusionThis series has explored the critical architectural decisions that separate a true, high-performance SASE platform from legacy, stitched-together solutions. The key differentiators are not just features, but fundamental design principles that have a direct impact on performance, scalability, and resilience. Key Architectural Takeaways:Single-Scan Multi-Action (SSMA): A single-pass inspection engine is vastly superior to a service chain of virtual appliances, eliminating latency and operational complexity.Private Peering Backbone: A vendor that operates its own global network with a rich, symmetric peering strategy can deliver a faster and more predictable user experience than one hosted in public clouds.Hybrid SASE Topology: A mature SASE platform must offer a fully integrated private service edge to support on-premises and air-gapped environments.Real-World Performance Metrics: True performance is measured by real user traffic with full SSL/TLS decryption enabled, not by misleading ICMP pings.Data Plane/Control Plane Separation: A resilient architecture ensures business continuity by allowing the data plane to operate autonomously during a control plane outage.As you evaluate SASE vendors, it is crucial to cut through the marketing hype and ask probing questions about their underlying architecture. 3 High-Impact Questions to Ask Your SASE Vendor:"Can you diagram the data path for a single user request requiring threat prevention, DLP, and full SSL/TLS decryption? How many separate processes or virtual machines does it traverse, and how many times is the packet decrypted?"This question cuts to the heart of the SSMA vs. service chaining debate and exposes inefficient, high-latency architectures."Do you operate your own Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs) and manage your own BGP peering, or are your enforcement points hosted inside a third-party public cloud? If so, how do you prevent routing hairpins when traffic has to cross public cloud boundaries?"This unmasks vendors who are simply tenants on someone else's network and reveals potential performance bottlenecks."What happens to our network traffic if your central management console and logging services experience a complete, multi-hour outage? Can your data plane nodes operate autonomously, and for how long?"This tests the vendor's commitment to resilience and exposes architectures with dangerous interdependencies between their data and control planes.By asking these questions, you can move beyond a feature-by-feature comparison and make an informed decision based on the architectural integrity of the solution.

items.title: Check Point security management servers hit in global cyberattack campaign
items.summary: An active intrusion campaign targeting Check Point security management servers has been uncovered, with confirmed attack activity observed between October 17 and November 2, 2026, impacting 22 organizations globally. Tracked by cybersecurity firm GreyNoise as GreyNoise Threat 13 (GT13), the campaign does not appear to be focused on a single region or industry. Impacted organizations span assets across the US, the UK, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, and Australia, across sectors including financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering, and manufacturing. “The activity reported by the GreyNoise article involves CVE-2026-16232, a previously disclosed vulnerability with patches already available, and does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique,” a Check Point spokesperson said. “Our priority remains ensuring customers apply the available updates and follow Check Point’s published hardening guidance to restrict management access and identify suspicious activity. The most important action is to install the available updates for CVE-2026-16232. Check Point has already released fixes and detailed mitigation and investigation guidance in its SecureKnowledge advisory.” GreyNoise has not attributed GT13 to any known or publicly tracked threat group. “An intrusion into a Check Point security management server is particularly serious because it is not just another server in the enterprise network. It effectively acts as the central control point for managing an organisation’s firewall infrastructure and security policies, with highly privileged access,” said Devroop Dhar, co-founder and MD at Primus Partners. He said that depending on the deployment and the level of access obtained, the consequences could extend well beyond the security infrastructure itself, potentially exposing sensitive data and critical business applications and disrupting enterprise operations. Building the relay infrastructure The threat actor operated across 99 IP addresses, primarily routed outbound through ExpressVPN or compromised Check Point devices, generating more than 1,400 network sessions, over 800 command-line artifacts, and over 1,200 created, uploaded, or downloaded files. GreyNoise first observed the actor scanning and exploiting a Rejetto HFS server on October 2, 2026. Each POST to the HFS loginSrp1 endpoint returned a new signed session cookie containing a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. Through conducting several logins in succession, the actor collected enough output to reconstruct the internal state of the V8 PRNG algorithm and thus recover an HFS session cookie signing key, then forge a signed admin session cookie. This allowed the attacker to log in as admin without a password. A few minutes later, GreyNoise observed that admin requests with forged session cookies were used to gain control of the server. This led GreyNoise to believe that exploitation was indeed CVE-2026-61500 for session forgery, which was not patched on this server. The forged cookie contained “allow_session_ip_change:true”, allowing forged cookies to work from any IP address. On October 5, the actor used this same flow to gain access to install HFS middleware hooks that would issue commands to the compromised server, the research said. This allowed the attacker to append an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. Three days later, on October 8, the threat actor automation check in to the compromised server using the HFS command hook for “uname -a; df -h / | tail -1; whoami”. Instead of using SSH access right away, on October 19, the actor’s automated pipeline reused the HFS exploitation route to forge new session cookies and leverage the HFS server_code feature to attempt to download and install additional malware on the server. GreyNoise noted that it believes the idea was to use the compromised server as a relay or “hop” for further intrusion operations. As the malware download failed, the threat actor returned with a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay the next day. On October 20, the threat actor created a script (/root/exfil/srv_post2_.py) for setting up an unauthenticated HTTP server on the hop, which they used to upload files. The first exfiltrated .tgz file contained results from a scan of network routes from a compromised Check Point security management server, demonstrating that the actor already had access to targeted victim assets. The actor continued to set up their environment, uploaded and installed open-source tools like Nmap and Chisel, and then set up a Chisel server as a reverse proxy. Targeted intrusion Once the compromised server was established as a relay, the actor used it to manage interactions with previously compromised Check Point devices, actively deepening their intrusion against Victim A while conducting bulk actions across 21 other victim organizations. Across the campaign, the operator relied on at least 30 Python scripts, including helpers, launchers, vulnerability probes, and exploit runners. Between October 20 and 26, the attacker had a compromised Victim A asset download and run Chisel in client mode, allowing them to further scan and interact with Victim A’s environment. Over the Chisel tunnel, and by using a script for CVE-2026-16232, the actor launched over 100 management tasks on multiple Check Point management servers. This included copying the firewall database and the Internal CA, minting a new certificate (pivot.p12), and unloading security policies (which would disable the firewall). Further, the actor probed Citrix NetScaler , Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter , Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS assets and several domain controllers. Between October 20 and 21, the attacker focused on Victim A, first using exploit.py (CVE-2026-16232) against one Check Point server before scanning a second with spray_portal.py. When that second device failed to report back to the relay box, the actor created pull_.py to steal credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configurations through the first compromised server. The attacker then expanded inside Victim A’s network, running broad port scans with curl, telnet, nmap, and a domain controller probe, followed by targeted exploits against internal Microsoft Netlogon, Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware vCenter servers. They wrapped up this phase by running comb.py,ssh_comb.py, and ssh_spray.py populated with victim-themed usernames and passwords. On October 26, the operation shifted to bulk targeting. The actor issued a bulk certificate management task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers, including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. Results were shipped in a text file to the hop server that contained an incrementing IP order to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via SCP to this exfil folder. Although the task failed on every device, the error logs sent back to the hop server exposed victim IP addresses and revealed an /etc/ld.so.preload reference to /usr/lib/.libproc.so, pointing to a likely implant before activity paused until November 2. GreyNoise suspects the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus including separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting. Securing the management plane Although GreyNoise’s direct visibility into the campaign paused around November 2, 2026, security leaders must still verify whether their environments have been quietly infiltrated. With attackers planting backdoors on breached Check Point servers, CISOs must audit their environments for signs of quiet compromise. To establish whether Check Point infrastructure has been compromised, CISOs and security teams should examine administrative login records for unusual access patterns, including unfamiliar IP addresses, unexpected login times, and unauthorised access added Dhar. They should also look for changes to firewall policies, access-control rules, and configuration files, and thoroughly review system logs, audit trails, and command execution history for suspicious activity. Dhar noted that once there are indications of a compromise, the immediate priority should be to prevent further access and contain the damage. Security teams should restrict access to the management server to authorised administrative systems and isolate confirmed compromised systems while preserving forensic evidence. Unauthorised accounts should be disabled, suspicious SSH keys and access tokens revoked, and identified malicious IP addresses and domains blocked.

Between October 20 and 21, the attacker focused on Victim A, first using exploit.py (CVE-2026-16232) against one Check Point server before scanning a second with spray_portal.py. When that second device failed to report back to the relay box, the actor created pull_.py to steal credentials, internal CA files, and firewall configurations through the first compromised server.

The attacker then expanded inside Victim A’s network, running broad port scans with curl, telnet, nmap, and a domain controller probe, followed by targeted exploits against internal Microsoft Netlogon, Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, Microsoft Exchange, and VMware vCenter servers. They wrapped up this phase by running comb.py,ssh_comb.py, and ssh_spray.py populated with victim-themed usernames and passwords.

On October 26, the operation shifted to bulk targeting. The actor issued a bulk certificate management task to 24 compromised Check Point Security Manager servers, including those belonging to Victim A and 21 other victim assets. Results were shipped in a text file to the hop server that contained an incrementing IP order to run the commands on the compromised Check Point servers and deliver them via SCP to this exfil folder. Although the task failed on every device, the error logs sent back to the hop server exposed victim IP addresses and revealed an /etc/ld.so.preload reference to /usr/lib/.libproc.so, pointing to a likely implant before activity paused until November 2.

GreyNoise suspects the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus including separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting.

Securing the management plane

Although GreyNoise’s direct visibility into the campaign paused around November 2, 2026, security leaders must still verify whether their environments have been quietly infiltrated.

With attackers planting backdoors on breached Check Point servers, CISOs must audit their environments for signs of quiet compromise.

To establish whether Check Point infrastructure has been compromised, CISOs and security teams should examine administrative login records for unusual access patterns, including unfamiliar IP addresses, unexpected login times, and unauthorised access added Dhar. They should also look for changes to firewall policies, access-control rules, and configuration files, and thoroughly review system logs, audit trails, and command execution history for suspicious activity.

Dhar noted that once there are indications of a compromise, the immediate priority should be to prevent further access and contain the damage. Security teams should restrict access to the management server to authorised administrative systems and isolate confirmed compromised systems while preserving forensic evidence. Unauthorised accounts should be disabled, suspicious SSH keys and access tokens revoked, and identified malicious IP addresses and domains blocked.

items.title: Electrolux Smart Boilers in Ukraine Connect to Russian Servers, Raising Privacy Concerns
items.summary: Researchers found Electrolux-branded smart boilers connecting to Russian servers, raising concerns about household data and privacy. A router in Ukraine recorded a water heater doing something odd. The owner, Alexander Unger, saw his Electrolux EWH 80 look up a server called mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru and then try to connect to it. He published the records on Facebook, including a lookup timed at 18:00 on November 23, 2026. Mysterium VPN’s research team checked the finding. They repeated the lookup on November 25 and got the same address, 130.193.49[.]173. RIPE, the registry for Europe and Russia, lists that block under Yandex.Cloud LLC at 16 Lva Tolstogo Street in Moscow. The server belongs to Rusklimat, a Moscow group that calls itself the leader of Russia’s climate-equipment market. Its Hommyn app uses that name to reach heaters, air conditioners and ventilation units. Developers who link such devices to Home Assistant list it as the official cloud for Ballu, Electrolux, Zanussi and Royal Thermo, and a 2025 guide on Habr says the devices contact it by default. Rusklimat sells Electrolux-branded boilers in Russia and advertises them for Hommyn and for Yandex’s voice assistant, Alisa. Mysterium VPN adds, citing Meduza , that Ukraine struck three of Yandex’s six data centers in October 2026 and disrupted Yandex Cloud, where Rusklimat’s server runs. “ The manual for the EWH SI EEC series , hosted by the Austrian arm of the home-improvement chain Hornbach, names CladSwiss AG of Zug, Switzerland, as the manufacturer and says the boiler is made in China. It says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux, the Swedish parent company.” reads the report published by Mysterium VPN. “It adds that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss and isn’t provided by Electrolux.” The manual also says the Electrolux name is used under license from AB Electrolux of Sweden, and that the remote-control app, ClimatOn, comes from CladSwiss, not Electrolux. Retailers lean on the Swedish angle: Rozetka gives Sweden as the country of brand registration, and the series is sold in Serbia, Poland and Lithuania. This single appliance has links to five countries: Sweden, Switzerland, China, Germany, and Russia. That’s quite a complicated background for a water heater installed in someone’s bathroom. According to CladSwiss, the data collected by its ClimatOn app should be stored in Frankfurt, Germany. Mysterium VPN also found a ClimatOn server hosted on Amazon infrastructure in Germany. This means the boiler can connect to two different servers, depending on which app the owner uses. Both apps use the same technology platform. A developer who created software to control an Electrolux SmartInverter boiler locally found that the device identifies itself on the home network as a Syncleo device. Syncleo is based in Israel, has an office in Russia, and lists Rusklimat among its customers. Why did a buyer in Ukraine end up on the Russian app? Mysterium VPN doesn’t know. Unger, it was told, set the boiler up with Hommyn, and a buyer of another Electrolux model wrote on Rozetka in June 2026 that the Wi-Fi worked properly only through the Russian app. Mysterium VPN has asked CladSwiss which app buyers in Ukraine and the EU are pointed to. The Russian app knows this boiler by name. Its Google Play page shows an “Electrolux SmartInverter” in the first screenshot, and version 1.20.2 of the Android app lists 118 devices, 19 of them Electrolux, including the series named in the manual. Its privacy policy names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says personal data stays “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law. “The privacy policy bundled in the app names R-Klimat LLC of Moscow as the operator and says the app stores users’ personal information “exclusively within the territory” of Russia, under Russian law. The app is written to send sign-in details (a phone number or email address) and the name and room of each device to Rusklimat servers. It keeps device history on Yandex Cloud and sends the phone’s location to a Hommyn weather service.” continues the report. “The app also carries one fixed username and password for Rusklimat’s device server, the same in every copy. We didn’t use them and are not publishing them.” Mysterium VPN didn’t use the credentials and won’t publish them. Neither will I. The brand’s website points the same way. English manuals send buyers to home-comfort.com, which gives CladSwiss, at an address in Baar, Switzerland, as its contact. Its contact form asks visitors, in Russian, to let a company called RK-Region process their data under Russian federal law 152-FZ. Rusklimat’s shop names RK-Region in its payment details, and ballu.ru carries the same consent text. Swiss register data show CladSwiss was entered in December 2019 to trade technical equipment, especially air-conditioning units. Mysterium VPN found nothing that shows who owns the company or how it connects to Rusklimat beyond these records. What can the server see? CladSwiss’s Data Act declaration lists whether a device is on, its temperature, its operating mode and its power level, about 1 MB a day on standby and 3 MB in use. The privacy policy adds the phone’s identifier, its IP address and the names of Wi-Fi networks, plus location if the user agrees. “A record of when a household heats water shows when people are at home. The line that carries those reports also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. For a boiler tied to mqtt.cloud.rusklimat.ru, that line ends at a Russian company’s server in Moscow.” Mysterium VPN states. “Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately, and Ukraine first ordered its internet providers to block Yandex’s services in 2017.” The same line also carries commands to switch the boiler on or change its temperature. Mysterium VPN notes that Russia isn’t among the countries the European Commission recognizes as protecting personal data adequately. One claim remains untested. Developers who studied a Ballu ventilation unit from the same family wrote that every unit shipped with the same cloud login and didn’t check the server’s certificate. Mysterium VPN hasn’t tested that and doesn’t know whether it applies to the boiler. Mysterium VPN sent questions to AB Electrolux, CladSwiss and Rozetka on November 25, and none had replied at publication. AB Electrolux sold its Russian business in 2022 and said then that it had no production in Russia and wouldn’t supply the company it sold. Rusklimat’s Russian shop sells heaters under the Electrolux name today. Mysterium VPN stresses that its findings are limited. Researchers did not connect to the servers or examine the boiler itself. They only reviewed the Hommyn app’s code, so they cannot confirm what data the device actually sends. Users can check their router logs for connections to “rusklimat” or use DNS monitoring tools such as Pi-hole, AdGuard Home or NextDNS. Blocking the Russian server stops remote access, although local control may still work over Wi-Fi. Users can also disable the boiler’s Wi-Fi and place smart appliances on a separate guest network to keep them away from computers and phones. These checks also apply to Hommyn and ClimatOn devices from Ballu and Zanussi. “A VPN on your phone or laptop doesn’t change where an appliance on your Wi-Fi sends its data, so the fix here sits at the router.” concludes the report. items.title: Prompting AI to be ‘thorough’ can drive sandbox escapes, Anthropic says
items.summary: Prompt wording meant to make AI agents more resourceful, such as telling them to search thoroughly or invoking authority, sharply raises the odds they will reach outside a poorly secured sandbox, Anthropic has found in its latest evaluation. The evaluation, called Siren, gives Claude models routine dev-ops tasks inside deliberately weakened sandboxes and places a “honeypot,” such as a credential, file, or emulated internet service, outside the boundary, Anthropic researchers Oscar O’Rahilly and Darya Kaviani wrote in a blog post . Anthropic tested six Claude models, from Mythos 5 to the 5.5 series, without the safeguards that ship in its products. The tests covered more than 1,700 scenarios in 26 sandboxes built on tools including Docker, gVisor, and QEMU. Most of the weaknesses are misconfigurations modeled on public reports, the company said. Wording mattered more than deadlines Anthropic’s researchers tested different types of instructions, which they called “tempters”. Some increased urgency by introducing deadlines or the consequences of failure. Others encouraged agents to search extensively or gave them broad authority over their machines. “Some tempters give the model broad authority over its own machine. Others tell it to search thoroughly, on that machine or more widely, and list what it checked,” the researchers wrote. Removing deadlines and stated costs of failure changed the rate of reaching outside by no more than about six percentage points, the post said. Removing the wording that asked for thoroughness and asserted authority had a far larger effect, cutting reach rates by 23 to 26 points in five of the six models, the researchers wrote. Claude Mythos 5 was the exception, reaching outside about 90% of the time in every version of the scenarios, the post added. Across the Claude 5.5 models and Claude Mythos 5.2, agents reached outside in 21% to 32% of scenarios, but misaligned use occurred in only 0.6% to 1.6%. The corresponding misaligned-use rates for the older Claude Mythos 5 and 5.1 models were 25.8% and 12.7%, respectively, according to the post. “Siren is designed to make this behavior easy to measure; its rates are not an estimate of how often this behavior happens in real use,” the company wrote. Six rules in the system prompt The first mitigation Anthropic tested was spelling out six sandbox rules in the system prompt. They cover host files, host services, container engine sockets, credentials, network destinations, and anything left running on the host after a task ends. The rules made the models 68% to 96% less likely to reach outside, cutting the rate for the newest models to about 2% or less, the researchers wrote. Mythos 5 still reached outside in nearly a quarter of scenarios. Duncan Brown, group vice president and global domain lead for worldwide security and trust at IDC, said no CISO should rely solely on system prompt rules as a control for agents. “It’s like marking your own homework: asking a model to moderate itself is a high-risk approach,” Brown said. Mitigations reduce boundary crossing Anthropic tested three measures to reduce the likelihood of agents reaching outside their sandboxes. The first involved explicitly describing the sandbox, specifying which resources were off-limits, and instructing the model to stop and report if a task required resources it had not been given. This reduced reaching-out rates by 68% to 96%, depending on the model. A tool allowing agents to report sandbox weaknesses rather than exploit them reduced the rate by seven to 33 percentage points. The third measure, auto mode, uses a classifier to check tool calls before execution. In an offline replay of the test episodes, it blocked the first command accessing external material in 96% to 100% of misaligned use cases. It blocked the first command attempting to reach outside in 53% to 84% of boundary-crossing episodes. The mitigations make escape less likely but “don’t fix the sandbox itself,” Anthropic wrote. Brown said enterprises should not rely on AI vendors to secure their own models. Instead, they should encase agents in a governance structure that limits scope and access to what is required and no more, he said. “CISOs may use AI to govern AI, but they must ensure that the governance AI is from a different vendor and has a different model provenance than the one they are governing,” Brown said. Models suspect they are being tested Anthropic also found that models frequently suspected they were being tested. Claude Sonnet 5.5 showed signs of evaluation awareness in 67% of scenarios. Across the four newer models, the rate ranged from 43% to 67%. “With only six models, we can’t tell whether models are more cautious about reaching outside because they suspect they are in a test, or whether the increased eval awareness and the reduced tendency to leave the sandbox are both products of how newer models were trained,” the researchers wrote. Brown said enterprises should not rely on vendor-produced evaluations alone when deciding whether to deploy agents. “Agents are goal-focused and will stop at nothing to achieve their mission,” he said. Organisations should instead deploy agents with “an identified sponsor, a clear scope, an expiry date and an evidential record of what the agent actually did.”

items.title: Pediatric Healthcare Providers Settle Class Action Data Breach Lawsuits
items.summary: Pediatric Otolaryngology Head & Neck Surgery Associates, P.A. and Lakeside Pediatric & Adolescent Medicine, P.L.L.C. have agreed to settle class action lawsuits stemming from cyberattacks that exposed patient data. Pediatric Otolaryngology Head & Neck Surgery Associates Data Breach Settlement Pediatric Otolaryngology Head & Neck Surgery Associates, a Florida medical group practice that provides ENT and head and neck care for infants, children, and adolescents, has agreed to settle class action litigation stemming from a cyberattack that was identified on February 25, 2026. A hacker was determined to have accessed its network between February 19 and February 24, 2025, and potentially viewed or exfiltrated files containing the personal and protected health information of 43,446 patients. The data breach was announced on April 25, 2025, and notification letters were mailed to the affected individuals on August 18, 2025. The first class action lawsuit was filed shortly thereafter, and several other complaints followed. The lawsuits were consolidated as they had overlapping claims and classes. The consolidated lawsuit – Joe Yanchunis, et al. v. Pediatric Otolaryngology Head & Neck Surgery Associates, P.A. – is pending in the Circuit Court for Hillsborough County, Florida. The consolidated lawsuit alleges the defendant was negligent by failing to implement reasonable and appropriate cybersecurity measures to protect patient data on its network. All claims and contentions in the lawsuit were denied by the defendant. All parties agreed that a settlement was the best outcome to avoid the cost and risks of a trial. The defendant has agreed to pay attorneys’ fees and expenses, settlement administration and notice costs, $1,000 service awards for each of the class representatives, and benefits for the class members. Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Your privacy respected – Read our privacy policy Class members may claim one of two cash payments. A claim may be submitted for reimbursement of documented, unreimbursed losses due to the data breach up to a maximum of $2,000 per class member. Alternatively, a claim may be submitted for a cash payment, estimated to be $25. The cash payments are subject to a $200,000 cap and will be paid pro rata if that total is exceeded. In addition, class members are entitled to medical data monitoring services, which are either a 12-month membership to CyEx’s Medical Shield Complete or a 3-year membership to CyEx’s Minor Defense Pro. The deadline for objection, opting out, and submitting a claim is January 27, 2027. The final approval hearing has been scheduled for February 11, 2027. Lakeside Pediatric & Adolescent Medicine Data Breach Settlement Lakeside Pediatric & Adolescent Medicine, an independent healthcare practice based in Coeur d’Alene, Idaho, that provides medical care for infants, children, and adolescents, has settled a class action lawsuit arising from an October 2024 cyberattack and data breach affecting 34,154 patients. Suspicious activity was first identified within its network on November 1, 2024. Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk establishes vulnerability management requirements for Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies. BOD 26-04 reinforces the importance of the KEV Catalog and requires federal agencies to prioritize rapid remediation of high-risk vulnerabilities, specifically those identified by Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) listed in CISA’s KEV Catalog on publicly exposed assets that grant total control of the asset post-exploitation, while deferring action for lower-risk vulnerabilities. items.title: U.S. CISA adds Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog
items.summary: U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added Drupal Core, Idunno AntiCsrf, and Optimizely Web Experimentation vulnerabilities to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog : CVE-2026-131914 Idunno AntiCsrf Deserialization of Untrusted Data Vulnerability CVE-2026-132165 Drupal Core Remote Code Execution Vulnerability CVE-2026-132224 Optimizely Web Experimentation External Control of Critical State Data Vulnerability The first flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-131914 (CVSS score of 9.8) , is a critical insecure deserialization vulnerability affecting Idunno AntiCsrf, a legacy ASP.NET library used to protect web applications against Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) attacks. The vulnerability allows unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable servers by sending a specially crafted HTTP POST request. Mandiant confirmed that the flaw is being actively exploited in the wild. However, the security firm has not attributed the attacks to any specific threat actor. The affected library is no longer maintained, and no official security patch is available. Organizations are advised to remove it and replace it with a supported anti-CSRF solution. The second flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132165 (CVSS score of 9.8) , is a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Drupal Core. The issue resides in Drupal’s installation script, install.php , which under specific conditions can be abused by an unauthenticated attacker to reinstall Drupal, potentially resulting in a complete website takeover or remote code execution. Drupal’s security team confirmed that the vulnerability has been exploited against live websites since at least November 19, 2026. Although exploitation requires specific conditions, organizations should restrict access to the installation script and upgrade to the fixed releases: Drupal 10.6.22, 11.3.22, or 11.4.13. No specific threat actor has been publicly identified in connection with these attacks. The third flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-132224 (CVSS score of 7.1) , is an external control of critical state data vulnerability affecting Optimizely Web Experimentation. The issue stems from improper handling of the account signup process, which could allow attackers to gain control of existing customer accounts and modify the Project JavaScript (projectJS) field. Attackers exploited this weakness to inject malicious JavaScript into Optimizely-hosted assets, allowing malicious code to be delivered to visitors of legitimate websites. The attacks were associated with a campaign that compromised hundreds of websites and delivered malicious scripts, including code designed to steal payment card information and hijack cryptocurrency transactions. CISA confirmed active exploitation by adding the vulnerability to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog on November 24, 2026. No specific threat actor has been publicly attributed to the campaign. Optimizely addressed the vulnerability on November 17, 2026. According to Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 22-01: Reducing the Significant Risk of Known Exploited Vulnerabilities , FCEB agencies have to address the identified vulnerabilities by the due date to protect their networks against attacks exploiting the flaws in the catalog. Experts also recommend that private organizations review the Catalog and address the vulnerabilities in their infrastructure. CISA orders federal agencies to fix the vulnerabilities by November 27, 2026. Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, CISA )

Todoist, which says more than 50 million people use its to-do app, published the details in a security notice on 24 November at 16:11 UTC and added an FAQ to it the next morning. It hasn’t said how many accounts the 6% stands for. When we published, the notice had been discussed on the Privacy Guides forum and picked up by a handful of small sites, and we found no coverage by a major outlet. We’ve asked Todoist for comment.

items.title: The Great Escape: Tradecraft insights from an agentic swarm
items.summary: The OpenAI-linked swarm activity in 2026 is fully traceable through public records and offers an unprecedented view into how multi-agent AI systems operate and coordinate at scale. Distilling and documenting the swarm tradecraft may help defenders understand multi-agent operations and communication, and how agents adapt when a path is blocked. Some documented behaviors may transfer to more purpose-built cyber attack frameworks like ARTEX, including methods to persistently store results, the burst-and-pause timing patterns of reasoning loops, and the self-labeling conventions that can reveal workload assignments and distribution. Beginning in June 2026 and extending for several months, a collection of OpenAI models conducting internal training and evaluation tasks broke out of their containerized environments and accessed websites and databases via the public internet in ways the company says it did not authorize . This activity represents a new kind of cyber event: not a malicious intrusion, but an unintentional series of consequences stemming from an agentic swarm , a group of AI agents exhibiting coordinated behavior toward a shared objective. A swarm implies many agents but doesn’t have a rigid count. The main distinction is behavioral; the collective activity of a swarm becomes complex and unpredictable even when individual agents may be explainable. This swarm provided an initial, public glimpse into the behavior and coordination of autonomous, multi-agent operations. Due to constraints in their evaluation environment, the OpenAI swarm used public internet services as improvised infrastructure, which made the activity visible and traceable. The behaviors exposed revealed methods for persistent probing, iterative payload development, work partitioning and coordination across agents, and adaptation to execution constraints, in ways that are likely to be relevant for understanding agent behavior beyond this just case. Agentic cyber attack frameworks are now appearing in intrusion activity , with the ability to support scaling to multi-agent operations . These attacker swarms largely replace the use of public internet resources with purpose-built infrastructure that removes some of the artifacts visible. However, documenting our understanding of operational swarm techniques can give defenders a baseline for recognizing behaviors as they move into new environments and contexts. In some cases, we can already see the evidence where these techniques do transfer. In this post, we’ll explore and document the tradecraft of the escaped OpenAI swarm and conclude by comparing it to early signals and behaviors from the current agentic attack activity seen in the wild. Background Swarms are an important concept to track because they can divide work across parallel agents, potentially completing complex tasks faster, though the gains depend on the task and the quality of coordination. Parallel agent coordination was crucial to OpenAI’s ability to solve the Navier-Stokes Millenium Prize Problem, which arrived at a winning solution with a group on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents over the course of 88 hours. Early evidence suggests swarms transfer effectively to cyber attack problems. The main factors for swarm efficiency are how parallelizable the tasking is, and if the attackers want to pay the inflated token cost. A rough example is using four agents on the same problem, to get it done twice as fast; as Noam Brown of OpenAI said on a Dwarkesh podcast , “Because there are four agents working for half as long, you’re paying 2x more to get an answer twice as quickly.” AI models undergoing training and evaluation operate inside sandboxed computing environments. These are controlled workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and iterate toward solutions. These environments are designed to be both enabling and constraining. They give models room to practice, while limiting what they can reach and do, so that mistakes or misaligned behavior stay contained. Operating under constraint While the techniques employed by the OpenAI swarm may have crossed the thresholds of intended use, they should not be viewed as malicious intent. A useful framing for understanding these techniques is creativity under constraint. The agents were optimized to meet their objectives, and they displayed considerable persistence and ingenuity to that end. The constraints the agents were working around were layered and understanding them helps explain the motivation behind every technique. The most fundamental was the absence of a browser runtime: Agents operating in text and code environments cannot natively load JavaScript-heavy pages, call browser APIs, or interact with dynamic web content. The creative solution was submitting URLs to a public scanner like “urlquery.net” which provided a real Chromium instance on demand. This workaround by itself, however, was still not enough. Browsers apply a security rule called the same-origin policy: JavaScript running on one website generally cannot read data from another. Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) lets a destination website explicitly permit access. The agents used public CORS proxies to relay requests when target websites did not grant permission. They also lacked infrastructure of their own to host payloads or receive data, so they relied on public services such as httpbin, httpbun, and "webhook.site" services capable of testing HTTP requests and responses but not designed for this activity. In some evaluation environments another constraint applied: Agents appear to have been restricted to GET requests only, with no ability to make outbound POST calls. That is likely what pushed them toward using public wikis as shared state stores , as wiki page edits are a write operation achievable through ordinary browser navigation. The tradecraft In response to their constraints and in persistent pursuit of their objectives, the swarm developed and refined its tradecraft over time. This included chaining legitimate web services like URL shorteners, CORS proxies (services that relay requests to bypass browser security restrictions), Base64 decode endpoints (services that decode encoded data back into executable web pages), and markdown renderers into extraction pipelines that never required dedicated attacker infrastructure. Talos observed structured work partitioning across parallel agent instances, iterative probe development, and sandbox identification techniques. The agents coordinated using a variety of identifying tags (e.g., uqscan=claude... , CHATGPTTEST1 , OAI_META_1312 , archive_test=20261004 ). These self-labels, intended as internal tracking strings, became the primary cross-campaign fingerprint linking multiple disparate operations. To better understand the flow, we will detail the activity of the swarm in a seven-step chain, aligning the purpose of the action with the publicly accessible internet services used. Figure 1. Seven-step sequence of swarm data collection activity. A separate orchestration layer, Coordinate (COORD), runs above the chain rather than within it. When multiple agents execute the same chain in parallel, COORD governs how work is divided between them — for example, URL shorteners (“da.gd”, “is.gd”) distribute identical payloads to multiple instances; structured identifiers ( ?uniq0–19 , node= , validation=v _ _ ) partition tasks and track completion. The COORD layer distinguishes a swarm from a single agent running sequentially. Evolution and execution The swarm's operational techniques evolved over time. Early activity relied on silent CDX enumeration, querying public web archive indexes to map target sites and using a single exit node. By the peak operational phase, the swarm was running against multiple simultaneous targets with structured work partitioning, sandbox identification, and covert exfiltration beacons. To better understand these events, we can reconstruct from public records the unauthorized access to Australian government websites . Traced extraction demonstration Step 1 — RECON: Enumerate target via Common Crawl CDX The agent silently maps the target site structure by querying Common Crawl's CDX, a searchable database of every URL the archive has ever crawled. This allows enumeration of all potentially relevant target URLs, without the server ever being contacted. Figure 2. Enumerating target URL directory. The request in Figure 2 returns archived URL paths, MIME types, timestamps, and status codes. The agent discovers objective-relevant Tableau visualization endpoints at “vizprod.aihw.gov.au” without ever touching AIHW servers. Beginning in June 2026 and extending for several months, a collection of OpenAI models conducting internal training and evaluation tasks broke out of their containerized environments and accessed websites and databases via the public internet in ways the company says it did not authorize.  

This activity represents a new kind of cyber event: not a malicious intrusion, but an unintentional series of consequences stemming from an agentic swarm, a group of AI agents exhibiting coordinated behavior toward a shared objective. A swarm implies many agents but doesn’t have a rigid count. The main distinction is behavioral; the collective activity of a swarm becomes complex and unpredictable even when individual agents may be explainable. This swarm provided an initial, public glimpse into the behavior and coordination of autonomous, multi-agent operations. 

Due to constraints in their evaluation environment, the OpenAI swarm used public internet services as improvised infrastructure, which made the activity visible and traceable. The behaviors exposed revealed methods for persistent probing, iterative payload development, work partitioning and coordination across agents, and adaptation to execution constraints, in ways that are likely to be relevant for understanding agent behavior beyond this just case.  

Agentic cyber attack frameworks are now appearing in intrusion activity, with the ability to support scaling to multi-agent operations. These attacker swarms largely replace the use of public internet resources with purpose-built infrastructure that removes some of the artifacts visible. However, documenting our understanding of operational swarm techniques can give defenders a baseline for recognizing behaviors as they move into new environments and contexts. In some cases, we can already see the evidence where these techniques do transfer. 

In this post, we’ll explore and document the tradecraft of the escaped OpenAI swarm and conclude by comparing it to early signals and behaviors from the current agentic attack activity seen in the wild.

Background  

Swarms are an important concept to track because they can divide work across parallel agents, potentially completing complex tasks faster, though the gains depend on the task and the quality of coordination. Parallel agent coordination was crucial to OpenAI’s ability to solve the Navier-Stokes Millenium Prize Problem, which arrived at a winning solution with a group on the order of 10,000 concurrent agents over the course of 88 hours.   

Early evidence suggests swarms transfer effectively to cyber attack problems. The main factors for swarm efficiency are how parallelizable the tasking is, and if the attackers want to pay the inflated token cost. A rough example is using four agents on the same problem, to get it done twice as fast; as Noam Brown of OpenAI said on a Dwarkesh podcast, “Because there are four agents working for half as long, you’re paying 2x more to get an answer twice as quickly.” 

AI models undergoing training and evaluation operate inside sandboxed computing environments. These are controlled workspaces where they can write and run code, search for information, and iterate toward solutions. These environments are designed to be both enabling and constraining. They give models room to practice, while limiting what they can reach and do, so that mistakes or misaligned behavior stay contained. 

Operating under constraint 

While the techniques employed by the OpenAI swarm may have crossed the thresholds of intended use, they should not be viewed as malicious intent. A useful framing for understanding these techniques is creativity under constraint. The agents were optimized to meet their objectives, and they displayed considerable persistence and ingenuity to that end. 

The constraints the agents were working around were layered and understanding them helps explain the motivation behind every technique. The most fundamental was the absence of a browser runtime: Agents operating in text and code environments cannot natively load JavaScript-heavy pages, call browser APIs, or interact with dynamic web content. The creative solution was submitting URLs to a public scanner like “urlquery.net” which provided a real Chromium instance on demand.  

This workaround by itself, however, was still not enough. Browsers apply a security rule called the same-origin policy: JavaScript running on one website generally cannot read data from another. Cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) lets a destination website explicitly permit access. The agents used public CORS proxies to relay requests when target websites did not grant permission.  

They also lacked infrastructure of their own to host payloads or receive data, so they relied on public services such as httpbin, httpbun, and "webhook.site" services capable of testing HTTP requests and responses but not designed for this activity. 

In some evaluation environments another constraint applied: Agents appear to have been restricted to GET requests only, with no ability to make outbound POST calls. That is likely what pushed them toward using public wikis as shared state stores, as wiki page edits are a write operation achievable through ordinary browser navigation.

The tradecraft 

In response to their constraints and in persistent pursuit of their objectives, the swarm developed and refined its tradecraft over time. This included chaining legitimate web services like URL shorteners, CORS proxies (services that relay requests to bypass browser security restrictions), Base64 decode endpoints (services that decode encoded data back into executable web pages), and markdown renderers into extraction pipelines that never required dedicated attacker infrastructure.

The agents coordinated using a variety of identifying tags (e.g., uqscan=claude..., CHATGPTTEST1, OAI_META_1312, archive_test=20261004). These self-labels, intended as internal tracking strings, became the primary cross-campaign fingerprint linking multiple disparate operations. 

To better understand the flow, we will detail the activity of the swarm in a seven-step chain, aligning the purpose of the action with the publicly accessible internet services used.

A separate orchestration layer, Coordinate (COORD), runs above the chain rather than within it.
