items.title: Securing Grandma's groceries with Pierre Cadieux
items.summary: This month, Amy is joined by Pierre Cadieux, Research Lead for Intelligence Efficacy at Talos. Pierre takes us back to his early days on help desks in the 90s, where learning to correlate logs between Windows and Unix systems sparked the curiosity that eventually led him to security. It’s a great look at how someone who has seen the industry evolve over decades stays grounded and keeps their edge. We also get into what’s kept Pierre at Cisco for nearly ten years. He talks about why he prioritizes the human impact of our work, the importance of knowing when to step away from the keyboard, and how his background in anthropology actually informs the way he approaches threat intelligence today. Amy Ciminnisi: I've known you since you were in Talos IR, which was not too long ago. But tell me a little bit about your professional journey, because I know that definitely was not the start of it. Pierre Cadieux: I worked at an ISP as part of the help desk back in the mid-90s. I was one of the people who people would call up and say, "Hey, I've got this computer I just bought, how do I get it on the internet?" I did a lot of learning about what TCP/IP was, what networking was, how to connect things via various different types of connections — whether it be an actual hard-coded network connection or a dial-up connection — and was able to get some expertise around guiding people through that process. Then I moved to a technology company in San Diego and worked on their help desk. One day, someone called me up and said, "You know how to read Linux logs, right? Or Unix logs, UCS logs, Linux logs." I said, "Yeah." They said, "You know how to use Windows — you're a Windows Server guy, too." I said, "Yeah." They said, "I need you to sit in this chair, look at these two screens — one is a Windows box, one is a Unix box. I need you to be a correlation engine." So, I looked at the timestamps for both of them, and helped to figure out what was happening because we were having an emergency, an incident, and they had nobody that could look at both. People at that point in time in this organization were very much, "I am doing just Unix things and only know Unix things. I am Windows things only. I only know one of those things." They didn't cross the streams. I could talk both. So I sat in the chair, I stared at both screens and I helped them to track the timeline of what was happening, which ended up being an intrusion exploiting a vulnerable SSH server that was compromised. That changed my course into security. I spent a number of years in internal security for a number of organizations and got into leadership positions, even CISO positions, leading security teams globally for financial services, for instance, and others. Then I moved into consulting and did that for a number of years as well. AC: Now you are on the TI&I team, and you also just started contributing to our Threat Source newsletter. What is it that kept you here after all those years? PC: I'm hitting my ten-year anniversary at Cisco in January. What keeps me at Cisco and Talos is the flexibility of my work. I'm able to, within most bounds, choose what I work on and how I get things done. I have a lot of flexibility in my workday, day-to-day. I work West Coast hours compared to most of my team members who are East Coast. So I sometimes work early shifts with them and am done by the early afternoon. Or sometimes I have to work with folks who are over in Asia Pacific, and I'm working later. The mission that Talos has resonates with me deeply. One of the things that I have seen along the way was not forgetting the why behind security, not forgetting the fact that what we are defending matters to people, not just to corporations, but to people who are affected by these things. In a newsletter intro, I mentioned that at one of the places I worked, they explained to me that a certain machine was super critical because it wrote the checks that get sent out to people who are expecting this check to come in weekly, monthly, whatever — that was going to be paying for grandma's groceries. And so that motivated me to make sure that box never went down and protect it in a very specific way. Even though it was something that probably should have been sunset and wasn't necessarily up to snuff from a security perspective, there are things we could do to protect it that would allow it to still function as we look for a better solution. At Talos, leadership gives us the space to execute that mission in a way that makes sense for us. Want to see more? Watch the full interview , and don’t forget to subscribe to our YouTube channel for future episodes of Humans of Talos.

items.title: GT13: AI-Assisted Hackers Target 22 Organizations Through Check Point Servers
items.summary: GreyNoise tracks GT13, an unattributed, probably AI-assisted campaign that hit 22 organizations via Check Point management servers. It may still be running. GreyNoise detailed an intrusion campaign against Check Point Security Management Servers. The company confirmed attacks between October 17 and November 2, 2026, and counts at least 22 victim organizations. It tracks the activity as GreyNoise Threat 13, or GT13. “GreyNoise recently discovered an intrusion campaign targeting Check Point Security Management Servers, with confirmed attack activity between October 17th and November 2nd, 2026, impacting at least 22 distinct organizations globally.” reads the report published by GreyNoise. The victims don’t share a country or an industry. They have assets in the United Kingdom, Ireland, France, the Netherlands, Greece, Germany, Austria, Bulgaria, Poland, India, Thailand, Vietnam, South Korea, Hong Kong, China, Australia and the United States. The sectors include financial services, energy, government, transportation, mining, engineering and manufacturing. GreyNoise cannot attribute the campaign to any known or publicly tracked threat group. The company also says it lacks enough information to identify the attackers’ motives or country of origin. GreyNoise tracked most of the activity through its Global Observation Grid, a network of sensors designed to attract and monitor scanning and exploitation attempts. These sensors work much like honeypots, but the company says they offer broader coverage. They allow researchers to observe entire attacks as they happen, rather than relying only on reports from victims. The attackers used 99 IP addresses, many of them temporary. These addresses belonged either to ExpressVPN exit nodes or to compromised Check Point devices. GreyNoise recorded more than 1,400 network sessions, 800 command-line artifacts, and 1,200 files that were downloaded, uploaded, or created. The part GreyNoise saw begins with a file server. On October 2 at 13:17 UTC, the actor started scanning and attacking a Rejetto HFS server through CVE-2026-61500 . Every POST to the loginSrp1 endpoint returns a signed session cookie that holds a “sid” value drawn from JavaScript’s Math.random() function. After several logins in a row, the actor had enough output to rebuild the internal state of the V8 random number generator. That gave it the key that signs session cookies, so it could forge an admin cookie and log in without a password. Two minutes later, GreyNoise saw admin requests carrying forged cookies, and the server hadn’t been patched. The forged cookie also carried “allow_session_ip_change:true”, which lets it work from any IP address. GreyNoise calls that perfect for an attacker behind a VPN or hopping between exits. On October 5, the actor used the same trick to install HFS middleware hooks that run commands, and it added an SSH key to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. On October 8, the attacker’s automated system ran a few basic commands to check the system, available disk space, and current user. The activity then stopped until October 19. On that day, the attackers used forged session cookies and the HFS server_code feature to try to download a Linux implant called “ZULT”. They did this despite already having SSH access to the server. The download failed. The attackers checked running processes, tested the download link with curl, and inspected the network settings. They could not work out why the implant had failed to download, so they returned the next day and used a direct SSH connection to continue setting up their relay. GreyNoise believes this failure may point to problems in a multi-agent system, suggesting that even automated tools can run into issues. On October 20, the attackers created a script to start an HTTP server on the compromised machine without requiring authentication. They then began uploading files. The first archive contained the results of a network route scan from a Check Point Security Management Server, showing that the attackers had already gained access to that system. They then installed Nmap and Chisel and configured Chisel to work as a reverse proxy. That made the HFS server a relay, or “hop” in GreyNoise’s wording. The actor used it to run its operations against Check Point devices it had compromised earlier, and to store the results. GreyNoise couldn’t determine when or how the actor got into those Check Point systems, only that it was there before the HFS compromise. Between October 20 and 26, the actor had a compromised machine in one victim’s network, which GreyNoise calls Victim A, download Chisel and run it as a client. Through that tunnel, a script for CVE-2026-16232 (a Check Point SmartConsole authentication bypass that leads to Run Script) launched more than 100 management tasks on several management servers. The tasks copied the firewall database and the internal certificate authority, minted a new certificate called pivot.p12, and unloaded security policies, which would switch the firewall off. The actor also probed Citrix NetScaler, Ivanti Connect Secure, VMware vCenter, Microsoft Exchange, Oracle TNS and several domain controllers. It ran exploits for CVE-2020-1472 (Netlogon), CVE-2023-4966 (NetScaler), CVE-2024-21893 (Ivanti), CVE-2021-26855 and CVE-2021-34473 (Exchange), and CVE-2021-21972 and CVE-2023-34048 (vCenter). GreyNoise also lists CVE-2025-5777, CVE-2026-41089 and CVE-2026-98432 among the flaws the actor used or tried to use. “The actor used Nmap , Chisel , Impacket , Paramiko and other Python tooling to perform intrusion activities against their victim assets, including attempts to perform internal reconnaissance, privilege escalation, and lateral movement.” continues the report. “The bulk of the adversary commands and interaction is too voluminous to dig into here, but we can expose some of the adversary’s TTPs by taking a glimpse at their tooling. The actor used at least 30 Python scripts, many of which were helpers or launchers for other scripts, and several of them were probes for vulnerabilities or runners of exploits. Excerpts are provided below to illustrate the more specialized tooling and workflows.” Password guessing played a part too. Scripts named spray_portal.py, comb.py, ssh_comb.py and ssh_spray.py carried common, default and weak passwords, plus usernames and passwords themed to the victim. The actor either knew its target or guessed well. When a second Check Point server wouldn’t report back to the hop, the actor wrote a pull script to steal its data through the first server. The script harvested credentials, internal CA files and the firewall configuration. It was named after the targeted device. On October 26 at 02:17 UTC, a bulk certificate task went out to 24 compromised Check Point servers: Victim A’s and those of 21 other victims. Results came back to the hop as text files that listed victim IP addresses in increasing order, so a loop was clearly running through them. GreyNoise never saw the actor send the task, which points to another part of its infrastructure. Every file showed an error, because the certificate task had failed. One message also flagged a preload error for /usr/lib/.libproc.so, registered in /etc/ld.so.preload, which may indicate an implant. GreyNoise saw no follow-up attempts, but the IP addresses in those files let it notify many victims, directly or through government partners. Check Point’s position, as reported by The Hacker News, is that this isn’t a new weakness. Sergey Shykevich, its director of threat intelligence, said the activity “does not represent a new vulnerability or exploitation technique”, since CVE-2026-16232 was disclosed earlier and patches exist. The company wants customers to apply updates, follow its hardening guidance to restrict management access and look for suspicious activity. By early November, other attackers had started scanning the hop and trying to abuse it. On November 2 at 02:28 UTC, the GT13 actor ran a script that checked the box for CVE-2026-98432, a Linux IPv4 use-after-free bug. It then used nftables to drop IPv4 packets with IP options that could trigger the flaw. The attacker did patch management on its relay, which is more than some victims managed. GreyNoise doesn’t read much into the clock. It saw no hands-on-keyboard activity between roughly 17:00 and 00:19 UTC, and nothing in the 05:00 hour, which fits a UTC+7 or UTC+8 workday. The malware domain newpayapp[.]com was registered on March 13, 2026, with the registrant state “Hai Phong” and country code “VN”, and GreyNoise treats that as a possible coincidence. The infrastructure clearly existed long before anyone noticed it. GreyNoise believes GT13 used AI tools to find vulnerable systems, develop exploits and automate attacks, although human operators were also involved. The company is sharing information with authorities and CERTs. Its monitoring stopped on November 2, but it warns that the campaign may still be active because attackers retain access to compromised Check Point devices. “We suspect the GT13 actor has a mature AI-enabled offensive apparatus. We believe the actor has separate agentic harnesses and systems weaponizing vulnerabilities, scanning for vulnerable assets, and automatically exploiting them to gather sets of systems that can be later used for operational relays or true targets.” concludes the report. “We suspect some of the foibles in the timeline reflect agentic offensive operations.” Follow me on Twitter: @securityaffairs and Facebook and Mastodon Pierluigi Paganini ( SecurityAffairs – hacking, Check Point)

items.title: How to protect against preinstalled Android malware
items.summary: Introduction Preinstalled malware on mobile devices is a major threat to user security and privacy. When we buy a new smartphone or tablet, we expect it to be ready to use and secure right out of the box. In some cases, however, devices ship with malware already on them. Such malware can do almost anything: display ads, collect personal data and credentials, track user activity, and more. Preinstalled malware can also turn the infected device into a tool for fraud, such as stealing credit card numbers or other sensitive information, causing financial loss and reputational damage. We’ve previously reported cases where users bought smartphones on marketplaces with malware already preinstalled. Over the past few months, however, several large organizations have encountered malware embedded in the firmware of mobile devices. The specific risks to corporate security depend on how the devices are used and on the company’s line of business. But because the Trojan sits in the device firmware, any app can be compromised, and the potential damage is hard to overstate. This post looks at the current landscape of preinstalled threats on mobile devices, the risks they pose to corporate users, and available countermeasures, including Kaspersky solutions. Landscape of preinstalled threats The total number of devices with malicious code found in their firmware or system apps keeps growing. According to Kaspersky Security Network, the number of such devices detected each month has increased more than 2.5-fold over the past year. Monthly number of Android devices with preinstalled malware detected by Kaspersky solutions, November 2025 — October 2026 ( download ) Several malware families are known to spread through firmware and system apps, the most common being Keenadu and Triada. According to our data, one or another of these two families was found on 88% of infected devices in the first ten months of 2026. The Triada backdoor (Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada) was discovered ten years ago and has remained popular with attackers ever since. Early versions of the malware actively exploited Android vulnerabilities to gain root access and the privileges they needed. At that time, Triada was often distributed as a regular app. Over time, however, Android introduced tighter restrictions, and attackers now mostly use the preinstalled version of this backdoor. Throughout 2026, users encountered about twenty markedly distinct variants. The most common ones were Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.ag and Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.z. The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads. Introduction

Preinstalled malware on mobile devices is a major threat to user security and privacy. When we buy a new smartphone or tablet, we expect it to be ready to use and secure right out of the box. In some cases, however, devices ship with malware already on them. Such malware can do almost anything: display ads, collect personal data and credentials, track user activity, and more. Preinstalled malware can also turn the infected device into a tool for fraud, such as stealing credit card numbers or other sensitive information, causing financial loss and reputational damage.

We’ve previously reported cases where users bought smartphones on marketplaces with malware already preinstalled. Over the past few months, however, several large organizations have encountered malware embedded in the firmware of mobile devices. The specific risks to corporate security depend on how the devices are used and on the company’s line of business. But because the Trojan sits in the device firmware, any app can be compromised, and the potential damage is hard to overstate. This post looks at the current landscape of preinstalled threats on mobile devices, the risks they pose to corporate users, and available countermeasures, including Kaspersky solutions.

Landscape of preinstalled threats

The total number of devices with malicious code found in their firmware or system apps keeps growing. According to Kaspersky Security Network, the number of such devices detected each month has increased more than 2.5-fold over the past year.

Monthly number of Android devices with preinstalled malware detected by Kaspersky solutions, November 2025 — October 2026 (download)

Several malware families are known to spread through firmware and system apps, the most common being Keenadu and Triada. According to our data, one or another of these two families was found on 88% of infected devices in the first ten months of 2026.

The Triada backdoor (Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada) was discovered ten years ago and has remained popular with attackers ever since. Early versions of the malware actively exploited Android vulnerabilities to gain root access and the privileges they needed. At that time, Triada was often distributed as a regular app. Over time, however, Android introduced tighter restrictions, and attackers now mostly use the preinstalled version of this backdoor. Throughout 2026, users encountered about twenty markedly distinct variants. The most common ones were Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.ag and Backdoor.AndroidOS.Triada.z. The latest Triada versions have two key distinguishing features: the ability to inject malicious functionality into any app on the device, system or user-installed, and a modular architecture that lets attackers tailor the malware to their current targets with additional payloads. Known modules can steal credentials for messaging and social media apps, intercept calls and text messages, replace links in browsers, siphon off cryptocurrency, and run a reverse proxy on the infected device. It’s worth stressing that by loading additional modules, attackers get virtually unlimited capabilities.

Keenadu is another preinstalled backdoor we discovered, which appeared relatively recently. The earliest known firmware version that contains this malware dates back to 2023. Even so, the number of devices infected with Keenadu is considerable: according to our data, more than 220,000 devices were infected in the first ten months of 2026.

Keenadu is similar to Triada in many ways, especially in its main architectural feature: once it’s on a device, attackers can download additional modules with any functionality and inject them into target apps. In most known Keenadu attacks, the malware was used for ad fraud, in particular to generate fake clicks. Technically, however, it can perform any action on the infected device. Notably, on first contact with the C2 servers, the backdoor versions we analyzed received a command to activate after about two and a half months. Until then, the malware showed no activity. This is probably meant to give the device owner time to install all the apps they need and settle into daily use, and to make the compromise harder to detect.

Other families of preinstalled malware exist, although they’re less common than Triada and Keenadu. They include Dwphon, Vo1d, and BADBOX. Their functionality is generally similar: mostly ad fraud and traffic redirection. Note that most cases involve phones and tablets, but preinstalled backdoors also threaten other types of devices. For example, Dwphon has turned up in the firmware of children’s smartwatches, and Vo1d samples in TV box firmware.

Corporate environment

We first saw an organization, rather than a home user, encounter preinstalled malware several years ago. That case involved the Dwphon malware. Over the past year, however, we’ve received more and more reports from different customers. In less than a year, several large organizations have come to us with the same request. After installing Kaspersky Endpoint Security for Android on brand-new, out-of-the-box devices, they saw detections of Keenadu or Triada and asked us to confirm that those detections were genuine.

Note that when we talk about corporate threats, we mean the Corporate Owned, Business Only (COBO) and Corporate Owned, Personally Enabled (COPE) usage scenarios, where the employee’s device belongs to the organization. The difference between these models is that COBO doesn’t allow personal use of the device (and usually blocks it at the software level). With COPE, the organization controls global settings but allows free personal use and, in some cases, even installation of third-party apps. By corporate environment, we mean primarily the setup with centralized procurement, where an organization buys all the devices it needs (hundreds, thousands, or even tens of thousands) for uniform use. This post doesn’t cover infections under the Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) model, where employees use infected personal devices they bought themselves to access company resources or for work communications.

Preinstalled malware appears on a new device as a result of a supply chain attack. Devices can be manufactured and flashed in different places. Likewise, different parties in the production process can create the firmware and prepare it for the device. Malicious code typically gets onto a device in one of three ways:

  1. The manufacturer installs the malware deliberately: the attackers control the entire production process and either sell infected devices cheaply under an obscure brand name or, conversely, pose as a well-known manufacturer, damaging that company’s reputation.
  2. A legitimate brand that makes the final device receives malicious firmware from a contractor acting in bad faith.
  3. A legitimate manufacturer builds the firmware in-house, but the build relies on an already infected base or code component. Here, no one directly involved in manufacturing knows the production chain has been compromised.

What risks do corporate customers face when they buy such devices? Based on the technical capabilities of preinstalled malware, we can identify the following main risks:

  • Degraded performance of infected devices: shorter battery life, overheating, and glitches in various apps. Some devices have even been known to play random sounds on their own.
  • Ads on devices, both visible to the user and hidden. They consume extra traffic and also connect the device to various websites, which creates a separate group of risks.
  • Account takeover in messaging apps, social media, and corporate resources: theft of credentials can damage the company’s reputation and lead to financial losses or even new attacks.
  • Direct financial losses, such as cryptocurrency theft.
  • Theft of confidential data and secrets: in effect, spying on corporate devices.
  • Use in a proxy botnet: the organization’s infected devices can relay arbitrary traffic to any internet resources.
  • Use in a DDoS botnet: infected devices can be enlisted to launch DDoS attacks on any target. Reputational risks come into play here as well.
  • External access to the corporate infrastructure through a proxy module. Infected devices are known to have been used as residential proxies to infect other devices on the same local network.
  • Device downtime: attackers who disable corporate devices in active use can disrupt operations.

Note that not all of the attack scenarios involving preinstalled malware listed above have been seen in real-world incidents. However, Triada and BADBOX, for example, have already expanded their functionality: besides displaying ads, they now steal accounts. We can therefore expect preinstalled malware to keep gaining capabilities that pose even higher risks.

Using Kaspersky solutions to mitigate risks

Mobile Device Management (MDM) is a separate category of solutions built to manage mobile devices, and it helps mitigate infection risks in corporate environments. With MDM, IT teams can centrally configure smartphones, tablets and laptops, enforce security policies, and control app installation. This significantly reduces the risk of infection caused by user actions, because it prevents a user from installing an APK from an attacker’s message, a malicious website, or a rogue app store listing.

However, these measures alone are not effective against preinstalled Trojans. Centralized mobile device management alone is not enough to contain threats like Triada and Keenadu. It must be complemented by protection that can detect malware, including any already present on a device before the company starts using it. Kaspersky Next can detect malware on Android devices, even in preinstalled apps, and alert administrators to any threats it finds. This allows spotting an infection on a device that nominally complies with corporate policies.

Triada detection report in the unified KSC console (screenshot in Russian)

Note that it’s technically impossible for either antivirus tools or the OS itself to remove preinstalled malware from the system partition. However, Kaspersky Next lowers the risk of buying a whole batch of devices and then finding a preinstalled Trojan that is hard or impossible to remove by reflashing. If Kaspersky Next detects malware like Triada or Keenadu, it alerts the IT administrator, who can then contain the threat by blocking the device’s internet access, clearing app data, rotating passwords, or locking the device entirely. Administrators can monitor and manage the infected device from the unified console of the Kaspersky Security Center.

Threat monitoring in the unified KSC console

Companies planning a mobile infrastructure should account for the risk of encountering preinstalled malware. Before ordering a large batch of devices, we recommend inspecting and pilot-testing sample units. We should stress that this measure is no substitute for installing security software on every device used in the organization. Even if the tests come out fine, an unscrupulous supplier may have deliberately sent clean units for inspection. Protection must also be continuous because, for example, the device update system could come under attack.

Manufacturers need to check devices and firmware code for malware just as customers do. Whether the firmware is written in-house or by a contractor, the result can contain malicious code, as we noted earlier. To detect preinstalled threats, you need a file scanning solution that can respond quickly when it finds malware. Kaspersky Scan Engine is one of the Kaspersky products designed for this task. The engine uses the latest detection technologies to identify a wide range of cyberthreats, including preinstalled ones. It integrates easily into a variety of workflows. For example, it can connect to a software build pipeline or any other system that needs to check files for malicious code.

items.title: Despite doom and gloom headlines, AI attacks are thin on the ground
items.summary: When Anthropic announced its Mythos AI model, it was touted as being so cyber capable that only a handful of organizations could have early access to harden their defenses before the public — and attackers — got their hands on the technology. Soon after, AI companies, one after the other, warned that their AI models were smart enough to discover previously unknown exploits and escape containment. And a new worldview took hold, that security organizations were soon to see a wave of new kinds of attacks, never seen before, and every company was at risk — unless it immediately started using the latest and greatest AI to defend against all these new threats. Has that happened? Well, kind of. What CISOs are seeing In the first quarter of 2026, RSAC asked Fortune 1000 CISOs whether they’d seen definitive evidence of AI-powered attack techniques being used against their companies, beyond social engineering, and 44% said yes. “We asked the same question in Q4 of a similar cohort,” says Laura Koetzle, RSAC’s head of community research. According to preliminary results — the survey isn’t complete yet — nearly 58% now say they’ve seen evidence of AI-powered attack techniques. As a result, the majority of CISOs are revamping their vulnerability management programs, according to the forthcoming survey. But they’re not upending how they approach cybersecurity, Koetzle adds. “The same foundational principles still apply.” The main difference today is in speed and quantity, she says. Lincoln Wallen, CTO at Framestore, an Academy Award–winning visual effects company, isn’t turning a blind eye to what AI could be used for by attackers. “We take the potential very seriously,” he says. But he’s taking an old-school approach to dealing with this new threat. “We’re putting a lot of emphasis on cleanliness, hygiene, and patching.” So far, the signs of AI use have been limited to more sophisticated phishing attacks, he says. “They feel anecdotally more well put-together, more convincing, involving many more disparate elements of data,” he says. “That’s the most concrete thing that we’ve seen.” To deal with that, the company has updated its anti-phishing training. Another area that Framestore is investing in is more efficient and prioritized patching and more frequent penetration testing. Enhanced productivity but familiar threats The data seems to support Framestore’s approach, even if the headlines don’t. Last week, headlines quoted Google’s announcement that “ the era of autonomous attacks had arrived ” — a reference to Google’s original blog post teaser to its latest AI Threat Tracker report. But in the actual report , John Hultquist, chief analyst at the Google Threat Intelligence Group, seemed to undercut this top line teaser, saying: “For the most part, attackers aren’t using new groundbreaking methods to break into systems — they are still going after known, unfixed issues, just with much greater speed and scale.” (Google later changed its headline to “ Outpace automated cyber threats with security built for nonstop defense .”) According to Google’s report, the mechanics of intrusion remain the same. Even attackers using new AI-powered attack frameworks are using them to leverage compromised credentials and unpatched systems. It’s the speed and scale at which these frameworks can be used that’s the challenge. In fact, using LLMs can even hurt the attackers, as the frameworks “trade stealth for velocity,” researchers say. The attacks can be “forensically noisy” and can hallucinate non-existent details or targets. “Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don’t.” Or, as Sergej Epp summed up as a takeaway from a recent Cloud Security Alliance CISO huddle call on autonomous attacks, “detecting these attacks is — at least for now — not the hard part. They make a lot of noise, like 1000 interns.” Austin Berglas, managing director and head of cyber operations at Nardello & Co., a global investigations firm, says he’s not seeing AI-discovered zero days or self-replicating AI agents out in the wild. “This is one of those examples that is still in the lab environment,” he says. Most attackers are using AI the way everyone does, he says. “Just like individuals use it for their daily productivity and efficiency, same with the bad actors. They’re able to scale, do it cheaper, do it quicker. And you’re seeing people who typically wouldn’t have the technical chops to do something, who are now able to do it because AI can do the technical side.” The industry is seeing evidence of faster weaponization of vulnerabilities, confirms Gartner analyst John Watts. “Where it starts to have less evidence is for fully autonomous attacks. What happened with Hugging Face is a fully autonomous attack, and that isn’t that common.” How CISOs should respond But if the wave of autonomous attacks and AI-powered malware hasn’t yet fully arrived, what should CISOs do given the reality on the ground? “The feedback that we get from our client base is that they believe there’s a lot of value in using the controls they already have,” Gartner’s Watts says. “The wake-up call for the practitioners is to get busy with the patching,” confirms Paul Webber, an analyst at Software Analyst Cyber Research, adding that security by obscurity is no longer an option. The biggest problem enterprises are facing, he notes, is that they need better automation to handle the increased workload, and the tools aren’t yet where they need to be. “People need more trust in the security tools so they can move from human-in-the-loop to human-on-the-loop towards fully autonomous response,” Webber says. “And that’s going to take some discipline, some standardization, and some proof in the efficacy of the security tools themselves. At the moment, they’re neither built to a specific standard or definition and people are being asked to make purchasing decisions without physical proof that the tools can do what they purport to do.” And, in some ways, the much-lauded defensive AI capabilities can make things worse — such as by exposing legacy vulnerabilities that companies now have to hurry up and patch, on top of their already large backlog. “This is a conversation that we’re actively having right now,” says Christina Powers, partner and cybersecurity consulting leader at West Monroe, a management consulting firm. “We’re working with a mid-sized bank, and they are just completely lost on how to keep up with the number of vulnerabilities that they got,” she says. “They’re sitting on millions of vulnerabilities. They don’t even know where to start. There’s a bit of analysis paralysis that’s happening because there’s so much information coming in.” The tools are improving all the time, Powers says, but she recommends security leaders not to wait for better technology to come along. “If you’re sitting and waiting, you become more of a target because you’re falling behind,” she says.

At the moment, they’re neither built to a specific standard or definition and people are being asked to make purchasing decisions without physical proof that the tools can do what they purport to do.”

And, in some ways, the much-lauded defensive AI capabilities can make things worse — such as by exposing legacy vulnerabilities that companies now have to hurry up and patch, on top of their already large backlog.

The tools are improving all the time, Powers says, but she recommends security leaders not to wait for better technology to come along.

“If you’re sitting and waiting, you become more of a target because you’re falling behind,” she says.

items.title: Maritime industry faces growing cyber threats as 50 ships targeted
items.summary: US authorities investigate suspected cyberattacks on up to 50 commercial ships, with Iran and Russia under scrutiny and Fortinet flaws involved. The United States is investigating a wave of cyberattacks targeting commercial vessels carrying oil, liquefied petroleum gas, chemicals, and other potentially hazardous cargo. According to a Wall Street Journal report , as many as 50 ships may have been targeted, with Iran emerging as the primary suspect. “The U.S. is investigating Iran ’s potential involvement in dozens of cyberattacks against energy tankers amid concerns that Tehran is widening the war with cyber operations and terror plots against Americans far from the Middle East.” WSJ states . “As many as 50 ships carrying oil, liquefied petroleum, chemical products and other explosive substances are believed to have been attacked, according to U.S. officials and others familiar with the matter.” US authorities are also considering possible Russian involvement. However, a Trump administration official told the WSJ that investigators have found no evidence linking Iran to the incidents and described four of the attacks as minor disruptions. The incidents reportedly involved both cyber intrusions and intimidation campaigns. Some vessels received bomb threats, ransom demands, and messages warning them against transporting US products. Other ships may have been compromised without their crews being aware of the intrusions. The US Coast Guard has reportedly deployed specialized cyber protection teams to at least four vessels approaching US ports to investigate and mitigate potential threats. The VL Prosperity and Kohaku were among the ships inspected after suspected compromises of their onboard networks. The attackers are reportedly exploiting vulnerabilities in Fortinet networking devices widely used across the maritime industry. In September, the US Coast Guard Cyber Command and the FBI issued a joint alert warning shipping companies about state-sponsored actors exploiting FortiGate vulnerabilities in maritime environments. The investigation also concerns vessels operating near Europe and Asia. One of them, the Vivit Africa LNG carrier, was reportedly targeted while transporting liquefied natural gas from the United States to Italy. The vessel experienced onboard system problems and received a bomb threat, although publicly available information does not establish that a cyberattack caused the technical incident. The incidents highlight the growing exposure of commercial shipping to cyber threats. Modern vessels rely on interconnected IT and operational technology (OT) systems to manage communications, navigation, and cargo operations. A compromise of onboard networks could disrupt operations, delay deliveries, and create safety concerns, although the reported incidents do not demonstrate that attackers gained control of critical navigation or propulsion systems. Alon Ayalon, co-founder of maritime cybersecurity firm Cydome, told the WSJ that most vessels have “less cyber protection than a midsize office.” Even without causing physical damage, cyber intrusions and threats can force shipping companies to suspend operations, undergo security inspections, and face costly delays. The investigation highlights the need for maritime operators to address exposed network devices, strengthen remote access controls, and improve the separation between IT and OT environments. items.title: The Governance Dead Zone: Why Your Private Apps Are the One Estate Nobody Audits
items.summary: For a decade, Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) solutions have answered a deceptively simple policy configuration question: “Can this user access this application?” But ask a slightly different question, “Should this user be allowed to access this application?” and most ZTNA deployments go quiet. There is a gap between “possible to configure” and “how do you know what policy to configure and maintain it over time”Walk into any large ZTNA customer deployment and you'll find a similar pattern: Overly permissive policies, each granting access that stays on until someone manually revokes it. It stays that way until someone remembers to go back and revoke it. Nobody does. Audits turn into spreadsheet archaeology. Security and IT teams can tell you that a policy exists; they often can't tell you who asked for it, who approved it, or whether it should still exist.With Autonomous user to app segmentation ZPA made policy configuration more intelligent and automated. Global Enterprises rushed to adopt it because it was unique and solved a major “able to implement” gap. Today, we're updating the Zscaler Private Access framework to include “Govern,” making Zscaler the first ZTNA vendor to make app-owner-driven governance a native pillar of the framework. This framework enables granular, time-bound and project-bound policies for better app governance: Hide. Segment. Govern. Shield. Deceive. Govern sits at the center of an architecture that controls connectivity and the defenses that block threats, because accountability for who should have access is the hinge that connects the two.Image1: Five pillars of ZPA Zero Trust framework The Driving Force Behind App GovernanceAsk most admins "Who owns this application, and who's allowed to approve access to it?" and the honest answer is: nobody knows. Here are some of the challenges including, 1. Admins never equipped to make the call: A small team of admins is typically responsible for access decisions across an entire application estate. In reality, they do not know that a given app belongs to the finance team or that an HR system requires a second sign-on before anyone can access it. Without a way to push that decision to the person who actually owns the application, admins are left guessing. Guessing doesn't scale past a few hundred apps, let alone a few thousand.2. Ownership remains the part nobody has solved: Even organizations that want to do this right hit the same wall: no admin, and no algorithm, can reliably say who owns a given application. AI can infer a guess from naming conventions or usage patterns, but a guess isn't an audit trail. Without an intelligent workflow that actually surfaces the right owner, access can't be delegated to the business, it defaults back to the team least equipped to decide.3. Third-party access: Vendors, contractors, and partners are routinely granted access to internal applications for a project or a support contract, and that access rarely has a named owner or an end date. In fact, breaches due to such access doubled year over year, from 15% to roughly 30% of all confirmed breaches, according to the most recent Verizon Data Breach Investigations Report.4. Manual operations to governance: So some organizations follow the approach of deny by default, grant on request. In theory, it looks like the fix. In practice, it creates a different failure. Users hit a wall with no idea which policy is blocking them and no clear way to ask for access. They open a ticket. They escalate. They ask a colleague to share credentials. Multiply that friction across thousands of users, and the "secure by default" collapses under its own policiesToday's access governance tools weren't built for this problemCurrent solutions assume the application is already known, already inventoried, already defined, with permissions someone configured manually. They have no visibility into what's actually running inside the network, so governance only works if developers remember to tell security teams what they deployed and follow policy when they do. They often don't. The result is a widening gap between what's actually accessible and what's actually tracked in the textbook definition of shadow IT.The industry has governance tools for two tiers of enterprise applications:SaaS and birthright apps, which are governed by Identity Governance and Administration (IGA) platforms (SailPoint, Saviynt, Microsoft Entra ID Governance, Okta, Omada) through the joiner/mover/leaver lifecycle.Privileged sessions (admin credentials, vaulted secrets, RDP/SSH to critical infrastructure), which are governed by PAM tools (BeyondTrust, Delinea).Between those two tiers sits a governance dead zone: the long tail of private, internally hosted applications behind ZTNA. They are too routine for privileged access management tools, yet far too custom and privately hosted to be visible to standard SaaS-centric identity governance connectors. Those applications make up the bulk of a typical ZTNA deployment, and until now, they have had no native governance at all.Image 2: The Governance dead zone that current solutions fail to address That's why Governance is such a powerful and critical component of a ZTNA strategy. Segmentation and shielding can limit the blast radius of a breach. Deception can detect lateral movement. But Governance is essential to address this need “Was this user supposed to possess access to begin with?”.Zscaler is uniquely positioned to answer that question across the full access landscape, because governance, segmentation, and privileged access all run through the same enforcement point: ZPA. SGA extends native governance to private apps, alongside Saviynt’s IGA for SaaS apps, and PRA for privileged infrastructure, giving Zscaler a governance story that spans all three tiers, not three disconnected tools.Introducing Zscaler Security Governance & Access (SGA)We're extending ZPA with Security Governance & Access (SGA), a governance layer that turns application segmentation from a static network boundary into a managed, accountable entitlement.With SGA, every application segment ZPA creates becomes an object that someone owns, and every access grant becomes a workflow, not a static rule. This governance, built natively into ZPA, provides four core capabilities:1. Resource OwnershipAny application segment can be mapped to a resource owner - an internal team lead, a director, a plant operator on a manufacturing floor or even a third party, as long as that individual is provisioned in the customer's Identity Provider. SGA decouples resource ownership from platform administration. A finance director can own access approvals for a finance app. A partner's PMO can own access approvals for a shared staging environment, without either needing ZPA admin credentials, console access, or security clearance to touch the fabric itself. The ZPA admin team never again becomes the bottleneck for every access decision. Approval authority goes to the people who know whether access is appropriate.2. Entitlement Workflows Per ResourceResource owners decide how access to their apps is granted. Options include birthright provisioning on join, auto-approval under defined conditions, or manual approval requiring a human sign-off. This mirrors the request-and-approve patterns IGA tools use for SaaS, now applied natively to private apps. For example: the Finance app grants read-only automatically to anyone in the Finance org; admin access requires the resource owner's manual approval.3. Just-in-Time Access by DefaultInstead of a static access policy that persists indefinitely once written, SGA grants access that is scheduled, time-bound, or request-triggered. Access expires by design, not by someone remembering. This is the foundational capability of SGA, and it's what makes governance enforceable rather than aspirational.4. Cross-Organizational Approval ChainsA common enterprise need - a systems integrator's engineer needs access to an application in the customer's environment. SGA lets the customer hold approval authority, even though the integrator's employee is the one requesting access. Ownership and approval don't have to sit inside the same company that's requesting access. ​​The audit trail captures both the integrator’s request and the customer's approval - a single compliance record spanning both organizations.How SGA Works Within ZPASGA is natively built-in to ZPA and therefore no upgrade, no App connector redeploy is required. Customers can deploy in weeks, not the 7–9 months typical of IGA rollouts. All configurations including ownership mapping, entitlement rules, and approval workflows happen in the ZPA administrative plane, and access decisions are still enforced at the broker, exactly where ZPA already enforces them today. What does change is how entitlement gets created. With SGA, once an owner defines a workflow, the entitlement is generated automatically as a byproduct of the approval process. This seamless scalability allows ZPA to efficiently manage thousands of applications and users across extensive enterprise deployments.Govern extends User-to-App segmentation in the framework. The granular segmentation provided by Zscaler's Autonomous User-to-App Segmentation empowers SGA to precisely govern access to each application. The two capabilities compound: better segmentation feeds better governance. A capability we're actively building, turning segmentation output into entitlement proposals the app owner can review and accept. Governing the Next Wave: AI Agents and Non-Human IdentitiesThe governance gap we've described so far applies to human users. The next version of the problem is larger and faster.Machine identities already outnumber human identities by more than 80 to 1 in most enterprises. AI and ML traffic across enterprise environments grew 91% year over year, spanning more than 3,400 applications, according to the Zscaler ThreatLabz 2026 AI Security Report. Also, Gartner predicts that by 2028, 25% of enterprise breaches will be traced back to AI agent abuse. These agents query databases, call APIs, trigger workflows, move data across systems, and spawn sub-agents, all at machine speed, often carrying credentials that are broadly permissioned and rarely reviewed.The same governance question applies: should this agent still have access to this application?SGA's architectural model is inherently suited for this. Every capability it provides for human users (ownership, entitlement workflows, time-bound access, audit trails) applies equally to any identity that accesses a private application through ZPA, including service accounts and, as our platform evolves, AI agents. In fact, the case for governance is stronger for non-human identities than for humans, because agents don't submit help desk tickets when access expires. They fail silently or find alternative paths, which makes expiration-by-default and owner-attributed access even more critical.Zscaler is investing broadly in this space. AI Protect, announced at Zenith Live 2026, delivers an enterprise agent registry, AI Access Graph (powered by our acquisition of Symmetry Systems), and inline guardrails for agentic workloads. Our partnership with Oasis Security extends non-human identity discovery and lifecycle governance across cloud, SaaS, and on-premises systems, connecting it to the enforcement layer that ZPA provides.SGA's role in this broader architecture is specific: it governs what an identity (human or non-human) can access within the private application estate, and ensures that access is owned, scoped, and time-bound. The discovery, risk-scoring, and lifecycle management of non-human identities themselves is where our AI Protect platform and ecosystem partners operate. Together, they provide a governance model that covers the full identity spectrum, from the contractor who logs in once a quarter to the AI agent that calls an internal API a thousand times a day.The IGA Opportunity: Extending Governance into Private AppsThe Identity Governance and Administration market is projected to exceed $10 billion in 2026. SailPoint, Saviynt, Microsoft Entra ID Governance, Okta Identity Governance, and Omada have each built deep connector ecosystems for governing access to SaaS applications, cloud infrastructure, and ERP systems. Their platforms automate provisioning, enforce separation of duties, run certification campaigns, and maintain the audit trails that SOX, HIPAA, and PCI DSS require.What those platforms have not been able to reach is the estate of private, internally hosted applications that sit behind a ZTNA broker. The reason is architectural. IGA tools govern applications they can see as discrete objects with defined entitlements. Most IGA platforms treat ZPA policies as network rules, not entitlement objects, which means they can't be discovered, requested, approved, or certified through standard IGA lifecycle workflows. SGA changes that. Zscaler has current API integrations with IGA platforms such as SailPoint and Saviynt and is working on growing these integrations to more vendors that allows these tools to extend governance to private applications. Here's how the combination works in practice:What the IGA Platform DoesToday: treats ZTNA policies as opaque network rules (if it integrates at all)What SGA ProvidesToday: ships natively inside ZPA, no integration required What the Combination DeliversTogether: ZTNA policies become first-class entitlement objects the IGA platform can discover, request, and certifyManages the identity lifecycle (join, move, leave)Maps each private app segment to a governable entitlementNew hires inherit the right private-app access on day one; leavers lose it the day they leaveRuns access certification campaignsExposes per-app ownership and approval metadata for reviewOne certification campaign covers SaaS, cloud, and private apps in a single reviewer queueAutomates provisioning and deprovisioningEnforces time-bound, workflow-driven grants at the ZPA brokerIGA requests a grant; SGA provisions it in seconds and auto-revokes when the clock runs outEnforces separation of dutiesProvides individual-application granularity (not subnet-level wildcards)SoD rules finally apply to the private app estate, not just SaaSMaintains audit trails for complianceRecords every request, approval, and expiration decisionA single evidence stream for SOX, HIPAA, PCI DSS — no spreadsheet reconciliation across systemsFor an enterprise running SailPoint or Saviynt alongside ZPA, the integration means that the same certification campaign governing access to Salesforce and Workday can now also cover the internally hosted finance application, the partner staging environment, and the legacy ERP system, all through the same governance console. For enterprises that don't yet run an IGA platform, SGA provides the governance fundamentals natively inside ZPA, so they can start governing private app access immediately and integrate an IGA tool later when their program matures.The point is that SGA and IGA are complementary, not competitive. IGA platforms bring deep identity lifecycle management. SGA brings the private application surface they've never been able to reach. An Open Invitation: Build With UsSGA is an essential function to protect private applications and requires an ecosystem.We are opening SGA's integration architecture to identity and governance partners. If you build an IGA platform, a PAM tool, an ITSM workflow engine, or any system that makes access decisions based on identity lifecycle events, we want to work with you to extend that decision-making into the private application estate that ZPA protects.The integration model is built on standard entitlement objects and workflow APIs. Each ZPA application segment, once SGA is enabled, becomes an entitlement that external platforms can discover, request, and govern through their existing lifecycle processes. We're designing for partners who want to give their customers a unified governance view across SaaS, cloud, and private applications, all without requiring those customers to manage a separate tool for each tier.We are actively inviting:IGA vendors (SailPoint, Saviynt, ConductorOne, Omada, Okta, Microsoft, and others) build connectors that bring ZPA-governed applications into their certification and lifecycle workflows.PAM vendors to extend privileged governance into the broader application estate that sits alongside (and often adjacent to) the sessions they already manage.ITSM and workflow platforms to integrate SGA's approval chains with their existing request management processes.Systems integrators and MSSPs to help joint customers design governance programs that span SaaS, privileged, and private application tiers in a unified model.If you're interested in partnering, reach out to our team or contact your Zscaler partner representative.Why This Must Be NativeA fair question: why build governance into the ZTNA platform instead of relying entirely on external IGA tools?Because the private application estate has characteristics that external tools struggle to address on their own. Private apps behind ZPA don't expose standard SCIM or SAML entitlement endpoints the way SaaS applications do. Their access is defined at the network segment layer, not the application layer. And the organizations deploying them may not have an IGA platform in place at all, particularly mid-market enterprises that have adopted ZPA for secure access but haven't yet invested in a full identity governance program.SGA solves for both scenarios. For enterprises with mature IGA programs, it provides the integration surface those programs need. For enterprises without one, it provides the governance fundamentals (ownership, workflows, JIT, audit trail) natively. Either way, the private application estate stops being a governance exception.The Evolved Five-Pillar FrameworkThe ZPA framework now reads: Hide. Segment. Govern. Shield. Deceive.Hide makes applications invisible to the internet. Segment isolates them so a breach in one place doesn't cascade. Govern ensures that access is owned, approved, time-bound, and auditable. Shield protects applications from exploitation. Deceive catches attackers who make it past every other layer.Govern sits in the center of the framework because it connects the architecture that controls connectivity with the defenses that detect and stop threats. Without governance, the two halves of the framework operate independently. With it, they share a common answer to the question every auditor, every CISO, and every board eventually asks: who has access, and should they?Zscaler Private Access with Security Governance & Access is now available in preview. To learn more about bringing governance to your private application estate, contact us or speak with your Zscaler account team. Identity and governance partners interested in building on SGA can reach our technology alliances team.

items.title: A Field Guide to OT Microsegmentation: Principles Before the How
items.summary: A few months back I wrote about why the factory floor feels unsecurable: uptime pressure that deprioritizes security, equipment that can't be patched on a normal schedule, and networks flat enough that one compromised sensor can reach almost anything else on them (Securing the Unsecurable: OT, IoT, and the Factory Floor)). The most common question back was some version of: okay, so how do we actually do this?Before the how, here are the principles. They hold regardless of what's enforcing them.If you've sat through a plant security review recently, there's a decent chance a diagram already exists showing your assets grouped into zones, with the connections between them marked as conduits. That's the model laid out in IEC 62443, the industrial cybersecurity standard most plants already reference to pass an audit. A zone is a group of assets that share common security requirements, in practice a shared trust level. A conduit is the controlled path connecting zones. The diagram usually gets drawn, signed off, and filed. Drawing it and enforcing it turn out to be two different projects, and most segmentation efforts stall in the space between them. Explain the threat, not the control or the standard. A rule that blocks a port, or a sentence about enabling microsegmentation, means nothing to someone running a line. A rule that stops a compromised sensor from reaching the equipment next to it means something. Lead with the second sentence every time, and let the standard stay in the audit paperwork where it belongs.Start small, but start. The segmentation projects that stall tend to share one thing: they were waiting for a complete asset inventory before writing a first rule. The ones that move usually skipped that step and started with whatever would hurt the business most if it went down. That's a much shorter list, and someone in the room already knows what's on it. Cut the obvious before building anything clever. Before writing an allow rule, block what has no legitimate reason to be on a plant network. The table below is a starting point, not an exhaustive list.Protocol / portWhy it's riskyField severity (1–10)*SMB (Server Message Block), port 445The protocol EternalBlue used to spread WannaCry; still a common path for lateral movement10NetBIOS, ports 137–139Used for name resolution; easy to spoof9Microsoft RPC (Remote Procedure Call), port 135A common step in ransomware chains9LLMNR/NBNS, port 5355Can be abused to poison name resolution and capture credentials9Telnet / FTP, ports 23/21Older protocols that send credentials in plain text8TFTP (Trivial File Transfer Protocol), UDP port 69No authentication; can be abused to tamper with device firmware8RDP (Remote Desktop Protocol), port 3389A common remote-access entry point, often missing multi-factor authentication7*Severity ratings reflect internal field patterns, not an external benchmark.On the plant floor this isn't just hygiene. Many operator stations and engineering workstations still running these protocols sit on older Windows builds that can't be patched without a vendor-approved change window, sometimes not at all. For machines like that, blocking these at the network layer is often the only control available. Know your order of operations. Before writing a rule, know what level it lives at and which level wins when two rules disagree. Three levels show up in nearly every platform: global rules written once for the whole environment, template rules scoped to a region or device type, and site rules written for one location. The implementation differs across vendors, so confirm how yours resolves a conflict before you assume it matches another one you've used.IEC 62443 answers a related but different question. When two zones carry different target security levels, the conduit between them has to meet the stricter of the two. That's about how tough the conduit's rules need to be, it has nothing to do with which rule fires first in your policy engine. Mix the two up, and you can end up with the wrong rule quietly winning out over the one meant to enforce the standard.Visibility is the foundation. You can't segment what you can't see, and OT visibility is its own problem with its own constraints. I went deeper on the discovery challenge itself in the prior post; this one assumes you've got a source of truth and focuses on what to do with it.Establish that source of truth, asset visibility tooling, a CMDB, a deployed Zero Trust Branch, whatever your environment already trusts. Once you have it, you need a way to label what's in it. I've seen customers use the native tags that come with their visibility tools. For instance, some write policy based on model number, Purdue level, or even the network the asset sits on. I've also seen customers apply their own custom labels after discovery, so the taxonomy fits their specific environment instead of whatever the tool shipped with.Whatever labeling you land on, use it to answer the questions that actually drive policy: which assets are critical to the business, which run end-of-life software nobody can patch, and which are both valuable and exposed at once. That last group is the one people miss. It's easy to flag an unpatched low-value device or a current high-value one; the overlap is harder to catch, and it's where the first rules should go.Map how things actually talk before deciding how they're allowed to talk. This step gets skipped because it feels slow, and it is slow. Depending on the tooling, mapping every real flow on a plant network can be a tedious, manual slog. Zero Trust Branch makes this easier by surfacing the flows for you rather than making you reconstruct them by hand. I'll go deeper on how in a follow-up post. For now, try to map these flows for your critical assets at least. Broad ports are fine at this stage. The goal is not breaking anything on the first pass, not precision. You can iterate and tighten later.Protect the crown jewels, and keep the whitelist scoped. This is where discipline tends to slip. Teams identify their critical assets correctly, then write a rule broad enough to recreate the same exposure they were trying to close, just at a smaller scale.Scoped doesn't mean minimal. It means every rule, even the ones applied everywhere, names a destination and a reason. A small set of infrastructure rules tends to show up at the global layer before any site-specific policy gets written: a vulnerability scanner reaching defined targets and ports instead of every port on every host, a security agent's callback scoped to that vendor's cloud destination and nothing else, a cloud inspection service scoped to its own destination, DNS and time services pointed at internal resolvers and time sources rather than the open internet, and domain controller authentication written as two separate flows, client-to-DC and DC-to-DC, instead of one symmetric rule.Moving past infra, every plant also has a short list of applications that run the business itself, and those deserve the same explicit treatment. Maybe it's a historian polling controllers for process data. Maybe it's an MES talking to line controllers, or a SCADA system polling remote terminal units. Whatever the application, name the asset, name the destination, name the protocol. Beyond zones and conduits. In zone-and-conduit terms, the critical asset group is the zone, and the scoped rule protecting it is the conduit. Getting from a flat network to zones and conduits is still a real win over where most plants started. The question worth asking is whether it's enough.IEC 62443 governs what crosses a zone boundary. It says nothing about what happens between two devices that already share one, and that's usually where lateral movement happens once an attacker gets a foothold. Treating the zone as the unit of trust made sense when the alternative was a flat network. It doesn't hold up against an attacker who only needs one opening and a clear path to the next device. We think OT security is heading past the zone as the unit of trust, toward the device. The question shifts from which zone a device belongs to, toward whether it has any legitimate reason to talk to the device next to it. A compromised sensor shouldn't reach the PLC three feet away just because they share a segment. The standard sets the floor: zones and conduits. Where we see things heading is past it: every device as its own enforcement boundary, every connection justified on its own terms. Observe before you enforce. Run new rules in a logged, non-blocking state first, and watch what still hits the old broad rule. In IT, a bad rule means a ticket and a rollback. In OT, it can mean a stopped line or a safety system doing something nobody predicted, with no quick fix available mid-shift. This step decides whether a program survives contact with production or gets shut off after the first outage.Iterate. Segmentation isn't a project with an end date. Correlate signals across sources over time, retire rules that haven't fired in months, and expect policy to drift as the environment changes.Wherever you're starting from, zones and conduits on a whiteboard or a network that's still flat, the move is the same: block the known bad, pick the handful of assets that would hurt the most if they went down, and write the first scoped rule around them. Everything else can wait.None of this requires waiting for a perfect inventory or a finished diagram. It requires picking a place to start and starting.

items.title: Cisco and OpenAI dispatch AI agents to shield vulnerable systems before permanent patches arrive
items.summary: Autonomous AI agents are rapidly and dramatically transforming the cybersecurity landscape for both defenders and adversaries. In hopes of giving security teams a head start and pitting machine against machine, Cisco and OpenAI have released a new open source project, dubbed Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”). The Shirudo platform launches small, temporary mitigations to help protect systems until patches can be deployed. AI agents can replace flawed code with fixed code, which human teams can test and approve (or not), then deploy, setting boundaries and holding onto the keys, with no need for a hard reset. The project has already been proven to block a Java4Shell exploit attempt against the search and analytics platform Elasticsearch, while the site continued to run as usual. Need to buy time “For years, we’ve treated security like a coat of paint,” Cisco president and CPO Jeetu Patel wrote in a blog post . “You first build infrastructure, then wrap security around it.” But, he asserted, this approach is “fundamentally mismatched” to AI. Security should live inside the infrastructure itself. “If protection sits outside the system, it’s always a step behind,” he said. He noted that AI agents are getting better at discovering security vulnerabilities; for instance, startup Calif used AI to help discover the PHP2Shell flaw and a major Java bug . Dovetailing with this, the agents themselves are both a risk vector and an adversarial actor. Attackers are using swarms of them to exploit discovered flaws; with both PHP2Shell and Java4shell, campaigns were underway “within a day of disclosure, if not before,” he pointed out. Flaws unfold over minutes and hours, as opposed to the days and weeks of the past, but permanent fixes take time to build, test, and roll out. “We need ways to shield systems and buy our teams time to get patches in place,” Patel said. Making the infrastructure secure from the start Shirudo combines Cisco’s infrastructure with OpenAI’s frontier models and AI research. It is built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF), which supports the running of small, sandboxed programs inside a Linux kernel without changing source code or loading additional modules. “This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems,” OpenAI explained in its blog post announcing the project . Speaking in their own language, guardian agents investigate and detect flaws and build shields, then test whether they stop the attack, all without disrupting the targeted service. The shields are cryptographically signed and only loaded when verified and deemed safe. Linux’s eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against safety rules, and kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes. Shirudo also uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being added or removed. All this takes place even if attackers have already gained access to a system. Further, self-defending agents can monitor for false positives, performance, and overall system health, and incorporate red-team findings and other feedback as well as signals for continuous improvement. Evidence backing every control travels across the system. The idea, according to Cisco and OpenAI, is to make the infrastructure itself secure by default. “We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer,” OpenAI wrote in its post. Shirudo in the wild Shirudo has its roots in Tetragon, an eBPF-based security platform developed and open-sourced by Isovalent, which was acquired by Cisco in 2024 . It is already incorporated into Cisco’s Live Protect capability. But Tetragon has been rewritten for the agentic era; its previous iteration pointed AI to human-oriented consoles, configuration files, and policy languages. In that workflow, the agent thought in machine code, which was then decoded for humans and processed, then translated back again into machine code. With Shirudo, agents interact in their natural language, which is code. “Agents are different,” Isovalent co-founder Thomas Graf and its chief open source officer Liz Rice noted in a blog post : They are very good at generating code, can absorb huge amounts of context quickly, and “[don’t] mind reverse engineering several million lines of assembly code.” In one controlled testing environment, researchers fed information about the Java4Shell vulnerability into Shirudo, which automatically created a shield against exploitation, generating a mitigation in Java bytecode which was injected into any Java app and added validation on the base64 input to guard against exploit attempts by threat actors. Graf and Rice explained that agent loops can either be tasked to actively search for new vulnerabilities on their own, or work off external sources like newly-available security disclosures. Agents can generate mitigation code, reproduce and validate exploits, and determine the most effective patching measures. This step is repeated until the agent identifies a successful path. The shield is then signed and securely rolled out to vulnerable nodes; it retires when a patch is installed. “This step is continuously monitored and repeated to achieve the highest possible security score while closely monitoring the health of applications,” Graf and Rice explained. It can be designed to be “more or less autonomous.” Once mitigation shields are deployed, the system employs a “hit” count of active exploitation attempts, so that exploits can be investigated on demand. Ultimately, the Shirudo project is only the beginning, Graf and Rice noted, but it already shows “true potential” and the hope is it will continue to evolve in the open source ecosystem. “We believe that building secure infrastructure for the AI era is an industry-scale problem,” they said. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, a permissive open-source software license approved by the Open Source Initiative. This allows anyone to use, modify, and redistribute software, including in proprietary or commercial products, with minimal restrictions. Its BPF programs are dual licensed under GPL and BSD. Developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators are encouraged to inspect the code, test outcomes, and contribute to the project’s development.
